papers.full_text: AbstractAfrican swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI) are among the most consequential infectious threats to global swine production because they combine major economic burden with fundamentally different transmission ecology, tissue tropism, and immune-pathological behavior. ASF is a highly lethal systemic disease characterized by macrophage tropism, immune dysregulation, environmental persistence, and severe trade and production consequences, whereas SI is a highly transmissible respiratory infection associated with recurrent herd-level morbidity, viral evolution, and zoonotic significance. Although these diseases differ markedly in biology and field presentation, both highlight the limitations of isolated pathogen-centered control strategies when implemented without integrated herd-level resilience measures. This meta-review synthesizes the cited literature into an evidence-based framework encompassing epidemiology, pathogenesis, surveillance, vaccination, biosecurity, herd management, supportive care, nutritional and immune-supportive measures, and host-directed regenerative approaches. Across the reviewed literature, the strongest field-supported evidence remains centered on surveillance, vaccination where applicable, biosecurity, and production-system management. At the same time, regenerative and host-supportive biologic strategies, including mitochondria-targeted peptides, thymic and organ-derived peptides, extracellular vesicle-based approaches, and stem cell-related therapies, demonstrate growing translational and immunomodulatory relevance within the broader context of immune resilience and recovery support. Comparative analysis further demonstrates that intervention priorities must remain aligned with disease biology: ASF control depends primarily on preventing viral introduction and limiting outbreak dissemination, whereas SI management benefits from integrated vaccination strategies, environmental optimization, mitigation of secondary bacterial disease, and continual adaptation to antigenic evolution. Within this framework, immune resilience is best understood not as a replacement for conventional disease control, but as a layered outcome arising from reduced infection pressure, preserved immune competence, regulated inflammatory responses, tissue recovery capacity, and supportive production practices.Keywords: African swine fever, biosecurity, herd management, host-directed therapy, swine influenza, transboundary 12.DiscussionThe comparative framing of ASF and SI provides a useful perspective for understanding how differences in pathogen biology influence disease control. ASF depends heavily on exclusion, early detection, biosecurity, surveillance, movement control and rapid containment because of its high mortality and environmental or wildlife-associated persistence. In contrast, SI is generally managed as an endemic respiratory disease through vaccination, herd immunity, strain surveillance and transmission control, although antigenic drift, strain mismatch and maternal antibodies can reduce vaccine effectiveness (27, 29, 30).Vaccination further illustrates this contrast. SI vaccination is already established in commercial practice, whereas ASF vaccination remains less mature and is limited by concerns regarding safety, cross-protection, DIVA capability, viral diversity and field consistency (14, 22). Therefore, ASF vaccination should complement, rather than replace, biosecurity and outbreak-control measures.Despite these differences, host factors influence disease outcomes in both infections. Immune competence, inflammatory regulation, age, co-infections, metabolic status and environmental stress can affect disease severity (80). Immune resilience should therefore be viewed as the ability to mount an effective antiviral response while limiting excessive inflammation and preserving tissue function. In ASF, host-directed approaches are more relevant as complementary research strategies for immune dysregulation, disease tolerance and recovery, whereas in SI, improving mucosal immunity and controlling pulmonary inflammation may more directly reduce disease severity and production losses (46).Important gaps remain in the development of immune-resilience strategies for ASF and SI. ASF research requires clearer protective immune correlates across viral genotypes and vaccine platforms, as well as improved understanding of immune evasion and disease tolerance, while SI research must address antigenic evolution, reassortment and the need for broader, more durable mucosal immunity. Future studies should validate interventions under commercial production conditions using standardized characterization, dose–response studies, controlled challenge experiments and independent replication, particularly for host-directed and regenerative approaches such as MO, PSC and NOP, whose efficacy in pigs remains unconfirmed. These strategies should be evaluated as complements to vaccination, biosecurity and antiviral control using standardized virological, immunological, clinical and production-related outcomes. 13.ConclusionAfrican swine fever and swine influenza remain highly appropriate diseases for comparative review because they reveal two different but interconnected dimensions of vulnerability in global swine health. ASF is defined by lethality, environmental persistence, and the central importance of preventing introduction and limiting spread after incursion (22, 64). SI is defined by high transmissibility, recurrent productivity losses, zoonotic significance, and the challenge of maintaining vaccine effectiveness in the face of viral evolution (6, 43). These differences justify different operational priorities but also support a shared resilience framework.On current evidence, the core pillars of control remain surveillance, biosecurity, herd management, and vaccination where biologically and operationally feasible (11, 12). Supportive care, environmental optimization, and nutritional adequacy are meaningful adjuncts, especially for SI, but they do not replace pathogen-specific control (10, 63). Host-directed peptides, mitochondrial strategies, and regenerative biologics are emerging areas of investigation that may contribute to resilience-oriented approaches, although their role in large-scale production systems continues to evolve alongside the evidence base (69, 79, 81). 1.IntroductionPork remains one of the most widely consumed animal proteins worldwide, making swine health central to food security, farm income, and stability of international agricultural trade (1). In parallel with rising demand, pig production systems have become more intensified, more interconnected, and in many regions more vulnerable to infectious disease due to dense animal populations, movement networks, and uneven biosecurity infrastructure. Viral diseases are therefore no longer only clinical problems at farm level; they are increasingly structural threats to productivity, market access, and regional food systems (2, 3).Among these threats, African swine fever and swine influenza occupy particularly important positions because they represent two distinct but complementary stress tests of modern swine systems. ASF is caused by African swine fever virus (ASFV), a large double-stranded DNA virus. Its severity depends on the interplay between viral strain virulence and host immune responses, as reflected in variations in clinical signs and mortality across diverse regional epidemiological scenarios (4). In contrast, SI is caused primarily by influenza A viruses (IAVs), which are segmented RNA viruses characterized by substantial genetic diversity and zoonotic potential (5). Clinically, SI is a highly transmissible respiratory disease associated with high morbidity, depressed growth performance, risk of secondary bacterial infection, and ongoing productivity loss at herd level (6). ASF, by contrast, is a severe systemic viral disease with mortality that can approach 100% in susceptible populations and remains defined by the absence of widely deployable curative treatment, the importance of environmental persistence, and the necessity of strict outbreak control measures (7, 8).A side-by-side analysis of ASF and SI is analytically useful because these diseases reveal different points of fragility in swine production. SI illustrates the burden of endemic circulation, antigenic evolution, and repeated respiratory outbreaks, whereas ASF illustrates the catastrophic consequences of a high-fatality transboundary disease in which prevention of entry is more feasible than therapy after establishment (9). Accordingly, this review adopts a meta-analytic perspective, with stronger emphasis on evidence hierarchy, biological plausibility, practical readiness, and the distinction between established intervention pillars and emerging approaches. 2.Scope and meta-review approachA key challenge in the literature is that interventions supported by strong field evidence are often presented alongside emerging biologic or regenerative concepts with evidence bases at molecular level, and without sufficiently clear stratification by evidentiary strength or practical relevance specifically in pig. That concern is particularly important in veterinary infectious disease because the practical usefulness of an intervention depends not only on mechanistic plausibility but also on cost, scalability, route of administration, herd-level logistics, and compatibility with commercial production (1, 10).In this meta-review, the literature is interpreted through four evidence layers. The first includes established field interventions such as biosecurity, surveillance, herd management, and commercially used SI vaccines (6, 11, 12). The second includes validated but context-dependent tools, such as emerging ASF vaccines that demonstrate strong pig challenge data but still face deployment and regulatory considerations (13, 14). Despite advances in ASF vaccine development and the authorization of some vaccine candidates for use in parts of Asia, there is currently no licensed ASF vaccine in the European Union. The third includes biologically grounded approaches supported by experimental and translational pig studies, including β-defensin-related strategies and other immune-modulating interventions (15, 16). The fourth includes host-directed and regenerative approaches, encompassing peptide-based, cellular, and signaling-modulation strategies that aim to enhance immune competence, tissue repair, and overall resilience under infectious challenge (17–19).For the present analysis, immune resilience is defined as the capacity of pigs and herds to limit infection, reduce disease severity, preserve immune competence, maintain tissue integrity, and recover functional productivity under pathogen exposure (20, 21). This definition deliberately avoids vague notions of generalized immune stimulation and instead emphasizes an interaction among pathogen pressure, innate and adaptive immune quality, inflammatory regulation, environmental load, and management structure. Within this framework, resilience is not a single therapy but an emergent outcome of layered control. 3.Epidemiology and global disease burdenAfrican swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI) are distinct infectious disease with markedly different epidemiological characteristics and represent major threats to the global porcine sector. ASFV and swine influenza A viruses differ profoundly in how they persist and spread across swine populations. ASFV persistence is shaped by environmental stability, contamination of fomites and pork products, wildlife reservoirs or interfaces, and human-mediated dissemination events, including long-distance jumps linked to transport and biosecurity breaches (22–25). In contrast, SI persists through endemic respiratory transmission, ongoing reassortment, antigenic drift, and repeated movement of viruses through swine populations interconnected by trade and production systems (26–29).These contrasting ecologies have practical consequences. ASF often behaves as a transboundary emergency in which the central question is whether the virus can be excluded or rapidly contained after entry (4, 30). SI behaves more like a constantly shifting endemic respiratory threat that repeatedly erodes production through cycles of infection, reinfection, and antigenic mismatch (6, 31). Both are damaging, but they operate on different temporal and epidemiological scales (Figure 1).Figure 1Comparative replication cycles of African swine fever virus (ASFV) and swine influenza virus (SIV). ASFV infects macrophages and replicates predominantly in the cytoplasm within perinuclear viral factories following endosomal escape and viral DNA release. Early and late gene expressions precede genome replication, virion assembly, maturation, and release via budding or cell lysis. In contrast, SIV infects respiratory epithelial cells and undergoes endocytosis followed by hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion and uncoating. Viral ribonucleoproteins are transported to the nucleus, where transcription and RNA replication occur, and progeny virions assemble at the plasma membrane and are released by neuraminidase-facilitated budding.Infographic compares African swine fever virus (ASFV) and swine influenza virus (SIV) replication cycles in pig cells. Steps for ASFV: attachment, endosome escape, DNA release, cytoplasmic replication, assembly, and release by budding and lysis. Steps for SIV: attachment, endosome escape and vRNP release, nuclear replication with RNA transcription, viral assembly, and release via budding and neuraminidase-mediated mechanisms. Both cycles are illustrated clearly with color-coded steps and labeled components.ASF spread since the emergence of the genotype II pandemic lineage has been characterized by persistent regional expansion, wildlife-associated maintenance, and episodic jump events across affected territories (4, 25, 32). However, ASFV exhibits substantial genetic diversity, with multiple genotypes circulating in Africa, while genotypes I and II have achieved broader geographical spread beyond the continent. Genotype I ASFVs were detected in domestic pigs in China in 2021, including low-virulence but efficiently transmissible strains associated with chronic infection (33). More recently, naturally occurring genotype I/II recombinant ASFVs have also been identified, including highly virulent and transmissible recombinant viruses detected in China (34). The co-circulation and recombination of genetically distinct ASFV lineages add further complexity to surveillance, disease control, and vaccine development. Consequently, this genetic diversity may impact vaccine efficacy, as cross-protection against heterologous ASFV strains and genotypes can be variable (35). Rathakrishnan et al. (36) demonstrated that a gene-modified genotype II live attenuated vaccine conferred complete homologous protection against genotype II ASFV, but only partial protection against genotype I and no protection against genotype IX, reflecting the need to consider circulating genotype diversity when evaluating the geographical applicability and breadth of ASF vaccines. In contrast, SI circulation is globally interconnected yet regionally structured, with North America and Europe acting as important source regions in long-term phylogeographic analyses, and live swine movement serving as a major driver of dissemination (5, 29, 37). The emergence of A(H1N1)pdm09 in 2009 illustrates the potential contribution of swine-origin influenza lineages to pandemic emergence. Following human-to-swine transmission, A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses can persist, evolve, and reassort with endemic swine influenza viruses, contributing to viral diversity and subsequent zoonotic risk (38). Markin et al. (39) and Zanella et al. (40) further demonstrated that continued circulation and evolution of these viruses in swine can increase genetic and antigenic diversity and maintain opportunities for subsequent zoonotic transmission. These patterns indicate that control strategies cannot simply transfer from one disease to the other; intervention design must reflect whether persistence is driven mainly by environmental durability and introduction events, or by respiratory circulation and viral evolution. For both diseases, current viral diversity emphasizes the importance of surveillance to detect newly emerging genotypes, reassortants, and variants that could alter transmission, vaccine efficacy, or zoonotic risk. 4.Transmission ecology and surveillance constraintsTransmission ecology sits at the interface between pathogen biology and farm practice. In ASF, circulation may involve domestic pigs, contaminated pork products, fomites, wild boar, and in some ecological context soft ticks (8, 22, 24). The importance of environmental survival means that virus introduction can occur even without direct pig-to-pig contact, which is why disinfection, feed safety, carcass management, and control of human and vehicle traffic are so important (11, 12, 23).In SI, by contrast, aerosol and direct-contact transmission dominate (41). High animal density, continuous flow systems, mixing of age groups, and repeated entry of new animals all favor persistence and spread (1, 37). Because influenza A viruses also reassort and accumulate antigenic changes, the epidemiological problem is not just the occurrence of outbreaks but the continual generation and circulation of immunologically variable viruses (26, 28).Surveillance limitations affect both diseases but in different ways. For ASF, variable reporting timeliness, inconsistent premise classification, and structural data gaps impede rapid detection and cross-country interpretation of outbreak patterns (32, 42). For SI, voluntary sampling systems, asymptomatic infections, and incomplete surveillance at the animal-human interface can underestimate prevalence and obscure zoonotic…

papers.title_original: Enhancing immune resilience in swine: a comprehensive meta-review of preventive and host-directed strategies against African swine fever and swine influenza

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on enhancing immune resilience in swine against African swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI). The central question is how to integrate preventive and host-directed strategies to improve disease control and reduce economic and health impacts on swine populations.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a meta-review that synthesizes the cited literature into an evidence-based framework. It includes studies on epidemiology, pathogenesis, surveillance, vaccination, biosecurity, herd management, supportive care, nutritional and immune-supportive measures, and host-directed regenerative approaches. The review explicitly mentions the use of standardized outcomes for evaluating interventions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that surveillance, vaccination where applicable, biosecurity, and production-system management are the strongest field-supported evidence for controlling both ASF and SI. Immune resilience is emphasized as a layered outcome arising from reduced infection pressure, preserved immune competence, regulated inflammatory responses, tissue recovery capacity, and supportive production practices.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There are conflicting findings regarding the effectiveness of SI vaccination, particularly due to antigenic drift, strain mismatch, and maternal antibodies. Additionally, the review notes that ASF vaccination remains less mature and is limited by safety concerns, cross-protection, DIVA capability, viral diversity, and field consistency. These limitations highlight the need for further research and standardization of outcomes.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should evaluate regenerative and host-supportive biologic strategies as complements to vaccination, biosecurity, and antiviral control. It also emphasizes the importance of considering circulating genotype diversity when assessing the geographical applicability and breadth of ASF vaccines. Operational priorities should align with disease biology, with ASF requiring strict outbreak control and SI benefiting from integrated vaccination strategies and adaptation to antigenic evolution.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines strategies to enhance immune resilience in swine against African swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI). It highlights the distinct biological and epidemiological characteristics of these diseases, emphasizing the need for integrated control measures. The review identifies surveillance, vaccination, biosecurity, and herd management as the most supported interventions. However, it also notes limitations in ASF vaccination due to safety, cross-protection, and viral diversity. The findings suggest that future research should focus on evaluating host-directed therapies and adapting strategies to the specific biology of each disease. The review underscores the importance of a shared resilience framework while acknowledging the need for tailored approaches based on disease-specific challenges.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 该综述的重点是增强猪对非洲猪瘟(ASF)和猪流感(SI)的免疫能力。核心问题是如何将预防性策略和 宿主 导向策略结合起来,以改善疾病控制并减少对猪群的经济和健康影响。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是一种元综述,将引用的文献综合成一个基于证据的框架。它包括对 流行病学、发病机制、监测、疫苗接种、生物安全、牛群管理、支持性护理、营养和免疫支持措施以及 宿主 导向的再生方法的研究。该审查明确提到使用标准化结果来评估干预措施。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 审查得出的结论是,监测、疫苗接种(如果适用)、生物安全和生产系统管理是控制 ASF 和 SI 的最有力的现场支持证据。免疫弹性被强调为由感染压力降低、免疫能力保留、炎症反应调节、组织恢复能力和支持性生产实践产生的分层结果。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 关于 SI 疫苗接种 的有效性存在相互矛盾的发现,特别是由于 抗原漂移、菌株不匹配和母源抗体。此外,审查还指出,ASF 疫苗接种 仍然不太成熟,并且受到安全问题、交叉保护、DIVA 能力、病毒多样性和现场一致性的限制。这些局限性凸显了进一步研究和结果标准化的必要性。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议未来的研究应评估再生和 宿主 支持的生物策略,作为 疫苗接种、生物安全和 抗病毒药物 控制的补充。它还强调了在评估 ASF 疫苗 的地理适用性和广度时考虑流行基因型多样性的重要性。操作重点应与疾病生物学相一致,非洲猪瘟需要严格的 暴发 控制,SI 受益于综合 疫苗接种 策略和对抗原 进化 的适应。

papers.title: From molecular evolution to the school health room: the role of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) in one health communication on cross-species influenza transmission in Norway

source_records.title: From molecular evolution to the school health room: the role of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) in one health communication on cross-species influenza transmission in Norway

papers.priority_tier_reason: 高相关性，且具备高等级研究设计、全文证据或较强数据库/引用支持
papers.full_text: AbstractHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have undergone an unprecedented expansion of host range since 2021, moving from wild birds and poultry into dairy cattle, domestic cats, and other mammals, with sporadic human infections in Europe and North America (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Rolfes et al., 2025). This expansion is underpinned by well-characterised molecular mechanisms of influenza A virus evolution — antigenic drift, gene segment reassortment, and receptor-binding adaptation — that shape the frequency and direction of cross-species spillover (McDonald et al., 2016; Steel and Lowen, 2017; Man et al., 2026). Norwegian wild-bird and mammalian surveillance data document recurrent incursions of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, and international risk assessments continue to describe low, but non-zero, human risk concentrated among individuals with close animal contact (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). Translating this fast-moving virological and epidemiological evidence into everyday protective behavior for children, adolescents, and families remains an underdeveloped link in pandemic preparedness, compounded by documented gaps in adolescent One Health literacy (Zucca et al., 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on the molecular basis of influenza cross-species transmission, the Norwegian epidemiological and One Health governance context, and established child- and family-oriented risk-communication frameworks, to argue that Norway’s community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) — who deliver near-universal, statutorily mandated contact with children and families through the helsestasjon- and skolehelsetjeneste — occupy a distinctive but underused position as One Health communication nodes (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). I outline a practical three-tier framework for translating zoonotic-influenza science into age-appropriate household guidance, critically appraise the feasibility, workload, training, and governance implications of this role, and identify priority gaps for future empirical and implementation research.Keywords: avian influenza, cross-species transmission, H5N1, health literacy, helsesykepleier, nordic public health, one health, pandemic preparedness Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2026.1965045/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 9.ConclusionThe molecular mechanisms driving the expanding host range of HPAI A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b are the subject of continuous, increasingly granular scientific characterization, and Norwegian wildlife and veterinary surveillance is generating an increasingly detailed picture of local risk. What remains comparatively underdeveloped is the corresponding public-facing translation infrastructure connecting this evolving evidence base to the households where behavior actually changes. Norway’s helsesykepleiere, by virtue of their statutory mandate and near-universal, longitudinal reach into families with children, constitute an existing but underused resource for this translation task — one consistent with, and potentially strengthening, Norway’s own stated One Health governance ambitions (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services; BeReady4Pandemics, 2025). Realizing this potential will require deliberate interdisciplinary collaboration between infection-prevention and virology research groups and the school health service, together with the evaluation research needed to ensure that any resulting communication genuinely improves family-level understanding and protective behavior, rather than simply adding to an already crowded preventive-health agenda. Realizing this potential is conditional on the workload, training, and governance safeguards above being resourced, not assumed cost-free. 1.IntroductionInfluenza A viruses remain among the most consequential zoonotic pathogens of the past century, with all major human pandemics traced to animal reservoirs, most often through reassortment of segmented viral genomes in avian or swine intermediate hosts (de Silva et al., 2012; Steel and Lowen, 2017). Since 2021, however, the epidemiology of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b has departed markedly from this historical pattern. Rather than remaining largely confined to wild birds and commercial poultry, clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have spread into an unprecedented range of mammalian species, including foxes, seals, mink, domestic cats, and, since March 2024, dairy cattle in the United States (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Kamel et al., 2025). Sporadic human infections have followed this mammalian expansion, and while sustained human-to-human transmission has not been documented, international risk assessments describe a dynamic and evolving situation that warrants continued vigilance (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Rolfes et al., 2025).This shift has practical consequences that extend well beyond veterinary and occupational medicine. Families that keep backyard poultry, own cats fed raw-food diets, or live near wild-bird habitats are now plausibly exposed populations, not merely bystanders to a distant agricultural problem (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a; Vaughan et al., 2026). Yet the substantial and rapidly evolving virological literature on cross-species transmission mechanisms is rarely translated into a form that reaches children, adolescents, and parents at the point where behavior change actually occurs — in the home, the farmyard, or the veterinary clinic waiting room. In Norway, one existing but underused channel for this translation is the corps of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere), who deliver statutorily mandated, near-universal contact with children and families through the child and youth health centers and school health service (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on (i) the molecular mechanisms underlying influenza A virus cross-species transmission, (ii) the global and Norwegian epidemiological landscape, (iii) Norwegian One Health governance and pandemic-preparedness structures, and (iv) established risk-communication and health-literacy frameworks for children and families, in order to outline a practical framework through which public health nurses can function as One Health communication nodes.Evidence for this mini review was identified through structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language literature published between January 2020 and August 2026, using combinations of the terms ‘H5N1’, ‘avian influenza’, ‘clade 2.3.4.4b’, ‘cross-species transmission’, ‘reassortment’, ‘One Health’, ‘risk communication’, ‘health literacy’, ‘helsesykepleier’, and ‘public health nursing’, supplemented by hand-searched reference lists and direct searches of institutional sources (FHI, Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Mattilsynet, WHO, EFSA, and CDC) for current risk assessments and guidance. Given the breadth of the topic and the mini review format, this is a narrative rather than a systematic review, and no formal quality-appraisal tool was applied. The specific search strings and retrieval steps are documented in Supplementary Search Record S1. 2.Molecular evolution and mechanisms of cross-species transmissionInfluenza A viruses possess a genome of eight discrete, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA segments, a structural feature that permits two distinct evolutionary pathways (McDonald et al., 2016). The first, antigenic drift, results from the gradual accumulation of point mutations introduced by the error-prone viral RNA polymerase during replication. The second, and epidemiologically more consequential for cross-species jumps, is reassortment: when two distinct influenza A viruses co-infect the same host cell, progeny virions can package a novel combination of the eight parental segments, generating genetically — and potentially phenotypically — distinct viruses in a single replication cycle (Steel and Lowen, 2017; Selective genome packaging mechanisms of influenza A viruses, 2021). Reassortment between avian, swine, and human lineages produced the reassortant strains responsible for the 1957, 1968, and 2009 pandemics, historically via swine acting as a permissive co-infection host, or ‘mixing vessel’ (de Silva et al., 2012).A second determinant of host range is the receptor-binding specificity of the viral hemagglutinin protein. Avian-adapted viruses preferentially bind α2,3-linked sialic acid receptors predominant in the avian gut and respiratory tract, whereas mammalian-adapted viruses, including human seasonal strains, preferentially bind α2,6-linked receptors characteristic of the upper mammalian respiratory tract. Single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin receptor-binding site, together with adaptive changes in the viral polymerase complex, can shift this binding preference and materially increase a virus’s capacity to infect and transmit within a new mammalian host (Man et al., 2026). Among these changes, PB2 substitutions such as E627K and D701N improve polymerase activity at mammalian upper-respiratory-tract temperatures and are recurrently detected in mammalian-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b genotypes, making them closely watched risk markers. Recent genotypes circulating in North American dairy cattle and companion animals, including B3.13 and D1.1, carry constellations of such adaptive markers, and ongoing genomic surveillance by joint WHO/FAO/WOAH assessment continues to track their evolution for signals of increased mammalian or human transmissibility (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Man et al., 2026). Because most reassortant or drift-variant genotypes carry fitness costs that limit onward spread, only a minority of spillover events establish sustained transmission chains in a new host — but the frequency of coinfection opportunities, and hence the statistical opportunity for a high-fitness variant to emerge, rises directly with the scale of the current panzootic. This technical surveillance information, while central to expert risk assessment, is rarely rendered in a form accessible to non-specialist audiences, a gap addressed later in this review.These molecular determinants of host range and transmissibility are not simply of virological interest. Because receptor-binding adaptation, polymerase mutation, and reassortment are the specific mechanisms that determine whether a spillover event remains a dead-end infection or acquires the capacity for onward transmission, they define the biological rationale for the tiered, exposure-specific communication framework proposed in Section 7: household guidance calibrated to the animal-contact pathways — raw feeding, wild-bird contact, dairy exposure — most likely to provide the coinfection or exposure opportunities described above. Framing the practical framework in these molecular terms is intended to keep the proposed nursing role anchored to virological evidence rather than to a generic exhortation to be alert to ‘bird flu’. 3.Current epidemiological landscape: global panzootic and the Norwegian contextSince its emergence in Europe in 2020–2021, clade 2.3.4.4b has become globally dominant, spreading across Europe, Africa, the Americas, and, more recently, Antarctica, with unprecedented mortality events in wild bird and marine mammal populations (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025b; Kamel et al., 2025). The detection of the virus in United States dairy cattle in March 2024 marked a further expansion: as of mid-2025, outbreaks had been confirmed in more than 1,000 herds across multiple states, with clinical signs in cattle including decreased milk yield, abnormal milk consistency, and reduced feed intake (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Morel et al., 2026). Between March 2024 and May 2025, a total of approximately 70 human cases of HPAI A(H5) infection were reported in the United States: 41 following exposure to infected dairy cattle, 24 to commercial poultry, two to backyard poultry flocks, and three with undetermined exposure (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025c). Most infections presented as mild conjunctivitis, occasionally accompanied by fever or respiratory symptoms; a minority required hospitalization, and one death occurred in a person with underlying health conditions exposed to a backyard flock and wild birds (Rolfes et al., 2025). A first pediatric case with an undetermined exposure source was identified in California in late 2024 (Zhu et al., 2025).Companion animals have emerged as an additional and household-relevant transmission pathway. Domestic cats appear highly susceptible to severe, often fatal, disease, typically following consumption of raw milk, raw pet food, or contact with infected wild birds; a global review identified more than 600 documented feline infections across 12 species and 18 countries since the emergence of clade 2.3.4.4b (CIDRAP, 2025; Sykes, 2025). In late 2024, a cluster investigation in Los Angeles County identified serologic evidence consistent with possible virus transmission from an infected domestic cat to a veterinary professional — one of 25 serosurveyed contacts among 139 potentially exposed persons, with no virus isolated from the human case — providing what may be the first, if unconfirmed, instance of cat-to-human zoonotic transmission for this clade (Vaughan et al., 2026). To date, no sustained human-to-human transmission of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses has been documented anywhere, and joint WHO/FAO/WOAH and European risk assessments continue to classify general population risk as low, with elevated risk restricted to those with direct occupational or household exposure to infected animals (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; European Commission / EFSA).Within this global picture, Norway has not been spared. Norwegian Veterinary Institute wild-bird and mammalian surveillance programs document recurrent clade 2.3.4.4b detections, including spillover into Norwegian foxes and seals, consistent with broader European surveillance trends reported by the European Food Safety Authority and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). As elsewhere, the general population risk in Norway is assessed as low, with the principal exposure pathway concentrated among individuals with occupational or hobbyist contact with wild birds, backyard poultry, or other domestic animals (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a) — a demographic that includes a meaningful proportion of Norwegian households with children, particularly in rural and peri-urban districts. 4.One health governance and pandemic preparedness in NorwayNorway has formally embedded One Health principles — the recognition that human, animal, and environmental health are interdependent — into its national approach to zoonotic disease and pandemic preparedness. The Norwegian Institute of Public Health identifies zoonotic influenza explicitly as a priority One Health working area, alongside food safety and antimicrobial resistance, and coordinates closely with the Norwegian Veterinary Institute and Norwegian Food Safety Authority on surveillance and risk communication (Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI), 2020). This institutional commitment is further reflected in Norway’s National One Health Strategy against Antimicrobial Resistance 2024–2033, which establishes cross-sectoral governance mechanisms that could, in principle, extend to influenza preparedness (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services), and in an independent country-profile assessment noting that Norway has integrated One Health principles into its broader pandemic preparedness and response framework through interdisciplinary task forces and improved cross-sector data sharing (BeReady4Pandemics, 2025).Notably, however, these governance frameworks are articulated predominantly at the level of surveillance coordination and inter-agency data sharing among human, animal, and environmental health authorities. None of the reviewed strategy or preparedness documents specify a defined role for frontline, community-based health personnel in the direct translation of One Health surveillance findings into household-level guidance. This represents an implementation gap between governance-level One Health ambition and the last-mile communication needed to change everyday behavior — a gap this review argues the helsesykepleier workforce is structurally well placed to help close. 5.The helsesykepleier as a one health communication nodeHelsesykepleiere are specialist public health nurses operating within Norway’s statutorily mandated child health and school health services (helsestasjons- og skolehelsetjenesten), providing near-universal, longitudinal contact with children and families from infancy through upper secondary school, encompassing routine health checks, vaccination programs, and structured health guidance for parents and, later, directly for adolescents (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This combination of near-total population reach, repeated contact over many years, and an existing mandate for preventive health counselling distinguishes the helsesykepleier role from generic public health messaging: unlike a one-off media campaign, the relationship is relational and cumulative, allowing guidance to be tailored to a given family’s actual animal exposures — for example, backyard poultry keeping, pet ownership, or proximity to wild-bird habitats — rather than delivered as an undifferentiated general warning.This structural advantage is particularly relevant given documented deficits in existing zoonotic-disease literacy…

full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have undergone an unprecedented expansion of host range since 2021, moving from wild birds and poultry into dairy cattle, domestic cats, and other mammals, with sporadic human infections in Europe and North America (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Rolfes et al., 2025). This expansion is underpinned by well-characterised molecular mechanisms of influenza A virus evolution — antigenic drift, gene segment reassortment, and receptor-binding adaptation — that shape the frequency and direction of cross-species spillover (McDonald et al., 2016; Steel and Lowen, 2017; Man et al., 2026). Norwegian wild-bird and mammalian surveillance data document recurrent incursions of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, and international risk assessments continue to describe low, but non-zero, human risk concentrated among individuals with close animal contact (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). Translating this fast-moving virological and epidemiological evidence into everyday protective behavior for children, adolescents, and families remains an underdeveloped link in pandemic preparedness, compounded by documented gaps in adolescent One Health literacy (Zucca et al., 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on the molecular basis of influenza cross-species transmission, the Norwegian epidemiological and One Health governance context, and established child- and family-oriented risk-communication frameworks, to argue that Norway’s community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) — who deliver near-universal, statutorily mandated contact with children and families through the helsestasjon- and skolehelsetjeneste — occupy a distinctive but underused position as One Health communication nodes (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). I outline a practical three-tier framework for translating zoonotic-influenza science into age-appropriate household guidance, critically appraise the feasibility, workload, training, and governance implications of this role, and identify priority gaps for future empirical and implementation research.Keywords: avian influenza, cross-species transmission, H5N1, health literacy, helsesykepleier, nordic public health, one health, pandemic preparedness

full_text_sections.conclusion: 9.ConclusionThe molecular mechanisms driving the expanding host range of HPAI A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b are the subject of continuous, increasingly granular scientific characterization, and Norwegian wildlife and veterinary surveillance is generating an increasingly detailed picture of local risk. What remains comparatively underdeveloped is the corresponding public-facing translation infrastructure connecting this evolving evidence base to the households where behavior actually changes. Norway’s helsesykepleiere, by virtue of their statutory mandate and near-universal, longitudinal reach into families with children, constitute an existing but underused resource for this translation task — one consistent with, and potentially strengthening, Norway’s own stated One Health governance ambitions (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services; BeReady4Pandemics, 2025). Realizing this potential will require deliberate interdisciplinary collaboration between infection-prevention and virology research groups and the school health service, together with the evaluation research needed to ensure that any resulting communication genuinely improves family-level understanding and protective behavior, rather than simply adding to an already crowded preventive-health agenda. Realizing this potential is conditional on the workload, training, and governance safeguards above being resourced, not assumed cost-free.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionInfluenza A viruses remain among the most consequential zoonotic pathogens of the past century, with all major human pandemics traced to animal reservoirs, most often through reassortment of segmented viral genomes in avian or swine intermediate hosts (de Silva et al., 2012; Steel and Lowen, 2017). Since 2021, however, the epidemiology of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b has departed markedly from this historical pattern. Rather than remaining largely confined to wild birds and commercial poultry, clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have spread into an unprecedented range of mammalian species, including foxes, seals, mink, domestic cats, and, since March 2024, dairy cattle in the United States (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Kamel et al., 2025). Sporadic human infections have followed this mammalian expansion, and while sustained human-to-human transmission has not been documented, international risk assessments describe a dynamic and evolving situation that warrants continued vigilance (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Rolfes et al., 2025).This shift has practical consequences that extend well beyond veterinary and occupational medicine. Families that keep backyard poultry, own cats fed raw-food diets, or live near wild-bird habitats are now plausibly exposed populations, not merely bystanders to a distant agricultural problem (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a; Vaughan et al., 2026). Yet the substantial and rapidly evolving virological literature on cross-species transmission mechanisms is rarely translated into a form that reaches children, adolescents, and parents at the point where behavior change actually occurs — in the home, the farmyard, or the veterinary clinic waiting room. In Norway, one existing but underused channel for this translation is the corps of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere), who deliver statutorily mandated, near-universal contact with children and families through the child and youth health centers and school health service (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on (i) the molecular mechanisms underlying influenza A virus cross-species transmission, (ii) the global and Norwegian epidemiological landscape, (iii) Norwegian One Health governance and pandemic-preparedness structures, and (iv) established risk-communication and health-literacy frameworks for children and families, in order to outline a practical framework through which public health nurses can function as One Health communication nodes.Evidence for this mini review was identified through structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language literature published between January 2020 and August 2026, using combinations of the terms ‘H5N1’, ‘avian influenza’, ‘clade 2.3.4.4b’, ‘cross-species transmission’, ‘reassortment’, ‘One Health’, ‘risk communication’, ‘health literacy’, ‘helsesykepleier’, and ‘public health nursing’, supplemented by hand-searched reference lists and direct searches of institutional sources (FHI, Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Mattilsynet, WHO, EFSA, and CDC) for current risk assessments and guidance. The first, antigenic drift, results from the gradual accumulation of point mutations introduced by the error-prone viral RNA polymerase during replication. The second, and epidemiologically more consequential for cross-species jumps, is reassortment: when two distinct influenza A viruses co-infect the same host cell, progeny virions can package a novel combination of the eight parental segments, generating genetically — and potentially phenotypically — distinct viruses in a single replication cycle (Steel and Lowen, 2017; Selective genome packaging mechanisms of influenza A viruses, 2021). Reassortment between avian, swine, and human lineages produced the reassortant strains responsible for the 1957, 1968, and 2009 pandemics, historically via swine acting as a permissive co-infection host, or ‘mixing vessel’ (de Silva et al., 2012).A second determinant of host range is the receptor-binding specificity of the viral hemagglutinin protein. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the gap in translating virological and epidemiological evidence of cross-species influenza transmission into actionable public health communication for children, adolescents, and families, particularly in the context of Norway’s One Health framework.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a mini review analyzing the molecular evolution of seasonal influenza viruses, the Norwegian epidemiological and One Health governance context, and risk-communication frameworks, focusing on community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) who interact with children and families through the helsestasjon- and skolehelsetjeneste.
analysis.methods: The methods involved synthesizing current literature on molecular determinants of host range and transmissibility, reviewing Norwegian epidemiological data, and examining established child- and family-oriented risk-communication frameworks to evaluate the potential role of public health nurses in One Health communication.
analysis.main_results: Recent genotypes circulating in North American dairy cattle and companion animals, including B3.13 and D1.1, carry constellations of adaptive markers. Norwegian Veterinary Institute surveillance programs document recurrent clade 2.3.4.4b detections, including spillover into Norwegian foxes and seals.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that reassortment, a process where two distinct influenza A viruses co-infect the same host cell and generate genetically distinct viruses, is epidemiologically consequential for cross-species jumps. This highlights the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to improve communication of surveillance findings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that Norwegian community-based public health nurses could play a critical role in translating complex virological data into accessible, actionable guidance for families, thereby improving pandemic preparedness and public health outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a review of existing literature and surveillance data, which may limit the depth of analysis. The evidence is moderate, as it relies on documented trends and expert assessments rather than original empirical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of community-based public health nurses in Norway in translating virological and epidemiological evidence of cross-species influenza transmission into public health communication for children and families. It highlights the importance of reassortment in generating new influenza variants and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to improve risk communication. The findings suggest that these nurses could be pivotal in bridging the gap between expert surveillance data and public understanding, enhancing pandemic preparedness. However, the study is limited to a review of existing literature and surveillance data, which provides moderate evidence for its conclusions.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一篇小型综述,分析了 季节性流感 病毒的分子 进化、挪威流行病学和 One Health 治理背景以及风险沟通框架,重点关注通过 helsestasjon 和 skolehelsetjeneste 与儿童和家庭互动的社区公共卫生护士 (helsesykepleiere)。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括综合有关 宿主 范围和传播性的分子决定因素的现有文献,回顾挪威流行病学数据,并检查已建立的面向儿童和家庭的风险沟通框架,以评估公共卫生护士在 One Health 沟通中的潜在作用。
elements_zh.main_results: 最近在北美奶牛和伴侣动物中流行的基因型(包括 B3.13 和 D1.1)携带一系列适应性标记。挪威兽医研究所 监测 计划记录了反复出现的分支 2.3.4.4b 检测,包括挪威狐狸和海豹中的 跨物种溢出。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,重配是两种不同的甲型流感病毒共同感染同一个 宿主 细胞并产生遗传上不同的病毒的过程,在流行病学上对跨物种跳跃具有重要影响。这凸显了跨学科合作的必要性,以改善 监测 研究结果的交流。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,挪威社区公共卫生护士可以在将复杂的病毒学数据转化为家庭可获得的、可操作的指导方面发挥关键作用,从而改善大流行的防备和公共卫生结果。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于对现有文献和 监测 数据的回顾,这可能会限制分析的深度。证据是温和的,因为它依赖于记录的趋势和专家评估,而不是原始的经验数据。

analysis_zh.main_results: 最近在北美奶牛和伴侣动物中流行的基因型(包括 B3.13 和 D1.1)携带一系列适应性标记。挪威兽医研究所 监测 计划记录了反复出现的分支 2.3.4.4b 检测,包括挪威狐狸和海豹中的 跨物种溢出。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,重配是两种不同的甲型流感病毒共同感染同一个 宿主 细胞并产生遗传上不同的病毒的过程,在流行病学上对跨物种跳跃具有重要影响。这凸显了跨学科合作的必要性,以改善 监测 研究结果的交流。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,挪威社区公共卫生护士可以在将复杂的病毒学数据转化为家庭可获得的、可操作的指导方面发挥关键作用,从而改善大流行的防备和公共卫生结果。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于对现有文献和 监测 数据的回顾,这可能会限制分析的深度。证据是温和的,因为它依赖于记录的趋势和专家评估,而不是原始的经验数据。

papers.full_text: Viral-bacterial co-infections represent a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality. In influenza virus infections, secondary bacterial pneumonia occurs in approximately 20–30% of cases and is associated with an increased risk of shock, mechanical ventilation, and even mortality. Bacterial superinfections are frequent causes of mortality in influenza severe infections and have been a major cause of morbidity and mortality also in COVID-19 patients. Staphylococcus aureus has been identified as one of the most prevalent bacterial pathogens among hospitalized and non-hospitalized patients who have tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza virus infections. Generally, antibiotic therapy is administered to at-risk patients to preclude bacterial over-infections by eliminating susceptible pathogens, increasing selective pressure favoring antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Due to the recognized public health problem of antibiotic resistance, the exploration of alternative therapies to counteract or prevent the development of serious virus/bacteria co-infections has become a critical research priority. The present study aimed to investigate the interactions between coronavirus or influenza A virus, and S. aureus in a co-infection model and to investigate the ability of a known antiviral/antibacterial compound, the bithiazole derivative MR335, to counteract the interaction between the two pathogens. The co-infection models were established using the pulmonary cell line A549 and the bronchial cell line BEAS-2B. The synergistic interaction between virus and bacteria were assessed through standard viral titration assays and bacterial adhesion and invasion assays. The bithiazole compound, MR335, showed both antiviral and antibacterial activity at distinct concentrations. In particular, it effectively counteracted the synergistic interactions between respiratory viruses and S. aureus at concentration that retained antiviral but not antibacterial activity. Notably, eradication of viruses impaired bacterial invasion, suggesting their synergistic cooperation and opening the way to alternative therapies that prevent bacterial superinfection without resorting to conventional antibiotics. Materials and methodsCell culture and viruses’ productionHuman lung adenocarcinoma cells (A549 cell line) were grown in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 0.3mg/ml glutamine, 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 μg/ml streptomycin. Influenza virus A/Puerto Rico/8/34H1N1 (PR8/H1N1), influenza virus A/California/7/2009/H1N1 (pH1N1), influenza A/parrot/Ulster/73 (H7N1) or parainfluenza virus Sendai type 1 (SeV) were grown in allantoic cavities of 11-day-old embryonated chicken eggs. Viral suspension was inoculated in the allantoic cavity and incubated for 48 h at 37 °C, then infected eggs were maintained overnight at 4 °C. The allantoic fluid was collected and clarified by centrifugation (2500xg for 30 min). The recovered virus was used for the infection of A549 cells. Allantoic fluid from uninfected eggs was used as reference for mock infection.Confluent monolayers of BEAS-2B were challenged with the Human Coronavirus (HCoV-229E) seasonal strain. After the viral adsorption, the cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and then incubated with the medium supplemented with 2% FBS for 24 h. Virus production was determined in the supernatants of the infected cells by TCID50 (tissue culture infectious dose 50%) assay. Briefly, MRC-5 (Medical Research Council cell strain 5) cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 2×104 cells/well for 24 hours at 37 °C in an atmosphere of 5% CO2. Subsequently, cell monolayers were infected for 1 hour at 37 °C, using 10-fold dilutions of the samples, previously collected upon infection. After viral adsorption, cells were washed with PBS and 100 μL of fresh medium supplemented with 2% FBS will be added to each well for 24 hours at 37 °C. The number of wells showing positive CPE was then scored. TCID50/mL will be evaluated by means of the Reed and Muench method.Bacterial strainsA collection strain of Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 6538 was used in the study. The strain was stored at -80 °C in glycerol stocks. For experimental procedures, S. aureus was cultured directly from glycerol stock on Triptone Soy Agar plates (TSA, Oxoid, Basingstoke, UK) and incubated aerobically overnight at 37°C. A colony grown on TSA plate was inoculated in Brain Heart Infusion Broth (BHI, Oxoid, Basingstoke, UK) and incubated overnight at 37 °C with agitation (180 rpm). The concentration of the overnight bacterial suspension was then measured spectrophotometrically (BioPhotometer, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany).CompoundsThe compound used was supplied in powder form, resuspended in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Chemical structure, published data and reference to its synthesis are reported in Table 1.Table 1Chemical structure of MR335.CompoundReference paper to synthesis, characterization and biological evaluation Chemical structure diagram of MR335, displaying an arrangement of rings, nitrogen, sulfur, trifluoromethyl, and carboxylic acid groups, with lines indicating bonds between atoms in the molecular structure. Martina, M. G.; Sannio, F.; Crespan, E.; Pavone, M.; Simoncini, A.; Barbieri, F.; Perini, C.; Pesce, E.; Maga, G.; Pedemonte, N.; Docquier, J-D.; Radi, M.ChemMedChem 2022, 17, e202200277.(compound 8b)IC50 (PI4KB) = 7.1 ± 0.65 μMCytotoxicity assayThe cytotoxicity of MR335 compound was assessed by using MTT (3-(4,5- dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide) reagent (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) assay on A549 cell line. In a 96-well plate, 200 μl of cell suspension (104 cells/well) were added to each well and the plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2. After 24 h, the culture medium was replaced with 200 μl of medium supplemented with MR335 compound at different concentrations (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 μM). Untreated cells were used as control. After 24 h of contact, the culture medium was replaced with 200 μl of fresh medium added with 3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) (5 mg/ml) (SERVA Electrophoresis GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany), then the plates were incubated for 4h at 37 °C, in a 5% CO2 atmosphere. Next, the culture medium with MTT was removed and 200 μl of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) were added to each well to dissolve the formazan crystals formed in the live cells. After 15 minutes of incubation, absorbance was measured at 570 nm, with the reference set at 620 nm, using the automatic microplate reader, Tecan Sunrise (Kumar et al., 2018). For solvent control, the cell viability was compared with the DMSO-treated cells, at the same volumes used for MR335 dilutions.Co-infection modelsCo-infection models between respiratory viruses and S. aureus were settled, referring to previous studies with some modifications (Oliva and Terrier, 2021; Sura et al., 2022; Goncheva and Heinrichs, 2023). In particular, co-infection models of S. aureus and PR8/H1N1 strain on A549 alveolar cell line and of S. aureus and HCoV-229E strain on BEAS-2B bronchial cell line were set up.For this purpose, A549 or BEAS-2B cells were seeded in 24-well culture plates at a concentration of 1,5×105 cells/mL, resuspended in complete DMEM medium and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. After 24 h of incubation, the cells were infected with PR8/H1N1 or HCoV-229E virus at MOI 0,1, in DMEM at 2% FBS, without antibiotics. After 22 h of viral infection, the cell monolayers were infected with S. aureus at a multiplicity of infection of 1 for A549 and 10 for BEAS cell line. The MOI was independently optimized for each cell line based on preliminary experiments aimed at identifying conditions yielding reproducible and quantifiable adhesion and invasion.The cells were then incubated for 2 h at 37 °C, 5% CO2. At the end of the 2 h of infection, supernatants were collected for viral titration assays. In addition, bacterial adhesion and invasion were evaluated. Cells were infected with S. aureus alone or virus alone in order to compare the results with those of the co-infection models. In parallel, the same experimental conditions were used to evaluate the efficacy of MR335 compound in interfering with virus-bacteria synergistic interactions. To this aim, the compound was added after viral adsorption and maintained for the following 24 h post-infection.Antiviral activity of bithiazole compoundConfluent monolayers of A549 or BEAS-2B cells were challenged with influenza virus A/Puerto Rico/8/34 H1N1 (PR8) or HCoV-229E, respectively, for 1 h at 37 °C. Then, cells were washed with PBS and incubated or not with MR335 compound diluted in medium supplemented with 2% of FBS for 24 h post-infection. Mock infection was performed with the same dilution of allantoic fluid. Viral titration was performed by TCID50 or Hemagglutination assay (HAU) method.In-cell western assayA549 cells were grown in 96-well plates (2 × 104 cells/well) and incubated with the supernatants of infected and treated cells for 1 h at 37 °C. After 24 h of infection, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Santa Cruz Dallas, TX, USA), permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and incubated with Odyssey Blocking buffer (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) for 1 h. Anti-Hemagglutinin (HA) or anti-influenza (Flu) antibodies (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA, USA) diluted in Odyssey Blocking Buffer were used to stain the cell monolayer at 4 °C overnight. Then, cells were washed and stained with fluorochrome-conjugated secondary antibodies together with Cell Tag (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA), a control for cell monolayer integrity, for 1 h at room temperature. The plates were analyzed by the Odyssey Imaging System (LI-COR, Lincoln, NE, USA). LI-COR Image Studio software was used to determine the integrated intensities of fluorescence, and the Relative Fluorescence Unit (RFU) was expressed as a percentage compared with untreated infected cells (100%).Real time PCRFor Hemagglutinin (HA) and coronavirus Nucleoprotein (N) relative quantification, total RNA was isolated from cell lysates (Total RNA Purification Plus Kit, Norgen Biotek, Thorold, ON, Canada) and used as a template for generating cDNA (iScript cDNA Synthesis Kit, Bio-Rad, Milan, Italy). An aliquot of the cDNA was subjected to 40 cycles of RT-qPCR amplification (95 °C, 10 sec; 60°C, 30 sec) using iQ SYBR Green Supermix and a LightCycler iQ 5 (Bio-Rad, Milan, Italy). Primer sequences are reported below:Influenza HA (Hemagglutinin) forward 5’ATTCCGTCCATTCAATCCAGAGG 3’ and reverse 5’ ACCATCCATCTATCATTCCAGTCC 3’; HCoV-229E Nucleocapsid (N) forward 5’-AGGCGCAAGAATTCAGAACCAGAG-3’ and reverse 5’-AGCAGGACTCTGATTACGAGAAAG-3’.Evaluation of antibacterial activity of bithiazole compoundThe antibacterial activity of the synthetic bithiazole compound was tested on the Gram-positive S. aureus strain. To evaluate the efficacy in growth inhibition, a bacterial suspension of S. aureus 1x108 CFU/ml was seeded in a 96-well plate in 200 μl of BHI broth containing different concentrations of the compounds (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 50 and 25 μM). As a positive control, the bacterial suspension was seeded in the absence of any substance. Likewise, to assess the effect of DMSO on bacterial growth, quantities of DMSO equal to those in which the compound was resuspended at the different concentrations were placed in contact with the bacterial suspensions. After 24 h of incubation at 37 °C, the contents of each well were collected, diluted, and seeded on TSA plates for bacterial colony counts.Evaluation of antibiofilm activity of bithiazole compoundThe antibacterial activity of MR335 compound was tested on the S. aureus ATCC 6538 biofilm. Bacterial biofilms were formed on a 96-well plate inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension and incubated 4 h at 37 °C. After the first 4 h of adhesion and microcolony formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and plates were rinsed with 100 μl of physiological saline (PS). Then, 100 μl of fresh medium were added and the plates were incubated at 37°C for an additional 20 h. The anti-biofilm activity of the substance was tested on both the 24 h formed biofilm and the forming biofilm. For the formed biofilm, after the 24 h incubation, the wells were rinsed with PS and 100 μl of BHI containing different concentrations of MR335 (500, 300 and 50 μM) were added.For the inhibition of biofilm formation, to better understand at which stage of biofilm development the substances acted, the experiment was performed under 3 different conditions: (B) a 96-well plate was inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension resuspended in BHI broth with the addition of different concentrations of the compound (500, 300 and 50 μM). After 4 h of biofilm formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and the plate was rinsed with 100 μl of PS. Then 100 μl of fresh BHI medium were added to each well and the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h; (BA) a 96-well plate was inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension in BHI broth with the addition of different concentrations of the compound (500, 300 and 50 μM). After 4 h of biofilm formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and the plate was rinsed with 100 μl of PS. Then 100 μl ml of fresh BHI medium containing the different concentrations of MR335 were added to the wells and the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h; (A) a 96-well-plate was inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension in BHI broth and after 4 h of biofilm formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and the plate was rinsed with 100 μl of PS. Then 100 μl of BHI containing different concentrations MR335 were added, and the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h.For each condition, after 24 h of incubation with the compound, quantification of biofilm biomass was assessed using the crystal violet (CV) assay (Radocchia et al., 2025).S. aureus adhesion and invasion assay on airway cell linesThe adhesive and invasive ability of S. aureus was assessed through the adhesion and invasion assay. To evaluate adhesion, after 2 h of bacterial infection, the wells were washed three times with PBS and cells were detached and lysed with 500 μL 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) per well and incubated for 5 min at room temperature (rt). The well content was then diluted in sterile PBS and seeded on TSA plates for bacterial colony counts. The colonies were counted and normalized to the number of eukaryotic cells present in the well. To evaluate the invasion ability of S. aureus, after 2 h of bacterial infection, the cells were washed twice with PBS before the addition of DMEM containing 200 μg/mL of gentamicin (CN) (Sigma-Aldrich Chemie GmbH, Buchs, Switzerland) and incubated at 37 °C for an additional hour to eliminate extracellular bacteria. Then, the cells were washed twice with PBS, lysed by adding 500 μL 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100 per well and incubated at rt for 5 min (Boudeau et al., 2003; Gagnon et al., 2013). After incubation, samples were collected, diluted and seeded on TSA plates for bacterial colony counts. The colonies were counted and normalized to the number of eukaryotic cells present in the well.Statistical analysisEach experiment was performed at least in triplicate. Statistical significance was determined using the One-Way ANOVA test on GraphPad Prism 9 statistical software package (GraphPad Software, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). To assess the statistical significance of adhesion and invasion assays, the Mann-Withney test was used. Data were expressed as means ± Standard Deviation (SD). Multiple comparisons of group mean differences were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test was used to compare paired samples. Differences were considered significant when the p-value was less than 0.05. ResultsMR335 exerts antiviral activity against different respiratory virusesIn the first set of experiments, based on preliminary results and on literature (Martina et al., 2021, Martina et al., 2022, Martina et al., 2024), we selected MR335 as the reference molecule to be studied in our models of respiratory viruses/bacterial coinfection.Firstly, we evaluated the cytotoxicity of the molecule on the A549 lung cell line by MTT assay, at different concentrations (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 μM). After 24 h of treatment, cell growth was evaluated and compared with that of untreated cells. Cell viability significantly decreased at MR335 concentrations ≥ 100 μM (p<0.001) (Figure 1A). The cytotoxicity test was also performed treating cells with DMSO at the same volumes used for each MR335 dilution, as solvent control curve. In this case, the results showed significantly reduced cell viability (p<0.005) for the volumes of DMSO used for the MR335 higher concentrations (500 and 400 μM) (Figure 1B). Based on these results, the range of concentrations chosen for antiviral activity was 10 to 60 μM, showing no cytotoxicity on A549 cell line (Figure 1). Next, the antiviral activity of MR335 was tested against different RNA respiratory viruses, i.e. human and avian influenza A virus strains, the seasonal coronavirus HCoV-229E and parainfluenza virus type 1. Although in the influenza A/PR8/H1N1 virus model of infection, the IC50 for MR335 was 17.3 μM (Supplementary Table S1), we chose to use for all the viruses tested in the study, the concentration of 40 μM to obtain the most reduction of viral titer. Permissive cells to respiratory viruses were infected and treated with the compound, as described in the Materials and Methods section. full_text_sections.results: ResultsMR335 exerts antiviral activity against different respiratory virusesIn the first set of experiments, based on preliminary results and on literature (Martina et al., 2021, Martina et al., 2022, Martina et al., 2024), we selected MR335 as the reference molecule to be studied in our models of respiratory viruses/bacterial coinfection.Firstly, we evaluated the cytotoxicity of the molecule on the A549 lung cell line by MTT assay, at different concentrations (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 μM). After 24 h of treatment, cell growth was evaluated and compared with that of untreated cells. Cell viability significantly decreased at MR335 concentrations ≥ 100 μM (p<0.001) (Figure 1A). The cytotoxicity test was also performed treating cells with DMSO at the same volumes used for each MR335 dilution, as solvent control curve. In this case, the results showed significantly reduced cell viability (p<0.005) for the volumes of DMSO used for the MR335 higher concentrations (500 and 400 μM) (Figure 1B). Based on these results, the range of concentrations chosen for antiviral activity was 10 to 60 μM, showing no cytotoxicity on A549 cell line (Figure 1). Next, the antiviral activity of MR335 was tested against different RNA respiratory viruses, i.e. human and avian influenza A virus strains, the seasonal coronavirus HCoV-229E and parainfluenza virus type 1. Although in the influenza A/PR8/H1N1 virus model of infection, the IC50 for MR335 was 17.3 μM (Supplementary Table S1), we chose to use for all the viruses tested in the study, the concentration of 40 μM to obtain the most reduction of viral titer. Permissive cells to respiratory viruses were infected and treated with the compound, as described in the Materials and Methods section. After 24 h, supernatants were collected, and viral replication was evaluated using different assays.Figure 1MTT assay on A549 cells treated with MR335 (A) or diluent solvent DMSO (B) at different concentrations (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 μM).Panel A shows a line graph with error bars for A549 cells, displaying absorbance at 570 nanometers versus compound concentration in micromolar, with a steep decline above 100 micromolar and significant difference indicated by four asterisks. Panel B presents a similar line graph for A549 cells, with a decrease in absorbance above 300 micromolar and three asterisks marking statistical significance at higher concentrations.As shown in Figure 2A, MR335 markedly reduced the cytopathic effect induced by influenza A strains infection compared to the untreated controls (indicated as PR8/H1N1 or pH1N1). Consistently, viral titers, measured by HAU assay, in the corresponding supernatants were strongly decreased compared to untreated infected cells (range of reduction in infectivity 75-91.7%) (Figure 2A, below images). The TCID50 assay also revealed a reduction of viral titer (about 0.5-1.5 log) in infected treated condition (Figure 2B).Figure 2(A) Representative light microscopy images acquired using a 10x objective, of PR8/H1N1 or pH1N1 induced cytopathic effect on A549 cells treated or not with MR335 (40 μM) for 24 h post-infection. The relative viral titer measured by HAU assay in the supernatants of A549 infected and treated cells is reported below the images. (B) TCID50 assay on MDCK cells by using the same supernatants analyzed in (A) The same plate was stained with anti-HA antibody and analyzed by Odyssey imaging.Panel A displays grayscale microscope images of cell cultures under five conditions: Mock, PR8/H1N1, PR8/H1N1 plus compound 335, pH1N1, and pH1N1 plus 335. Cells infected with PR8/H1N1 or pH1N1 appear disrupted, while those treated with compound 335 resemble controls. HAU per milliliter is reduced with compound 335. Panel B shows fluorescent images of multi-well plates stained for viral antigen from the same groups, with reduced green fluorescence and decreased TCID50 per milliliter in wells treated with compound 335, indicating lower viral activity.The antiviral activity was also confirmed by using ICW assay in A549 cells that had been infected with either the PR8 or pH1N1 strains. Specifically, the viral infectivity of the supernatants of infected and MR335 treated A549 cells, were used to infect a fresh new cell monolayer. The expression of viral protein (hemagglutinin; HA) was quantified as a percentage of relative fluorescence units (RFU) analyzed by ICW, as described in the material and methods section. As shown in Figure 3A, with respect to untreated conditions (considered as 100%), the percentage of HA RFU was reduced by 35% and 30% in PR8 or pH1N1 treated conditions, respectively. Consistent with these findings, RT-qPCR analysis revealed a significant reduction in HA mRNA expression in MR335-treated PR8- or pH1N1-infected cells (Figure 3B).Figure 3(A) In Cell Western (ICW) assay on A549 cells infected with supernatants of PR8/H1N1 or pH1N1 treated or not with MR335 (40 μM) for 24 h.
