papers.full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. Intra-family BSAs Can be active against multiple serotypes, genotypes or strains of a particular virus species. For example, mosnodenvir is active against all dengue virus genotypes (family Flaviviridae) by blocking the interaction between viral proteins NS4B and NS3. Intra-family broader-spectrum activity may span several viruses within one genus of a particular family without extending to other genera. For example, the non-covalent, non-peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor ensitrelvir is active only against members of the genus Betacoronavirus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), SARS-CoV-1 and human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43), but not against members of the genus Alphacoronavirus (such as HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63) within the family Coronaviridae. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article inhibitors) or active against one or more (but not all) genera of a viral family (Box 1). The need for broader-acting antivirals and their desired spectrum of activity are mostly defined by the particular (clinical) context (Boxes 2 and 3). For viruses that cause a high number of annual cases (for example, RSV), there might be a sufficiently large market, and thus incentives, to develop virus-specific drugs. Conversely, there might be no or less financial incentive to develop virus-specific drugs for viruses that cause a rather limited number of cases but that col- lectively, within their genus or family, are responsible for a substan- tial clinical burden (for example, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, EV-D68 and EV-A71 that all belong to the genus Enterovirus). In this case, the development of antivirals that are broadly active across the entire Enterovirus genus (pan-Enterovirus; category intra-family BSAs) represents a more realistic approach. In the context of epidemic or pan- demic preparedness, access to pan-family and cross-family BSAs may be particularly important, as it cannot be predicted which viral family a newly emerging pathogen (‘virus X’) will belong to. Given the extensive genetic diversity and distinct replication strategies of viral families, the development of a single cross-family drug with potent activity against all RNA virus families is likely to be unrealistic. Rather, a more feasible strategy may be to establish a portfolio of different types of BSAs that collectively provide, either alone or in combination, coverage across the RNA virus landscape. BSAs may also be valuable in the context of viral co-infections, in which a single drug could simultaneously target two (or more) viruses14,15. Beyond the spectrum of activity, BSA development must be guided by clearly defined target product profiles16. To have a meaningful clinical impact, BSAs (or combinations thereof) should ideally be highly efficacious, be orally available (preferably once daily dosing), be safe for a broad patient population (preferably including pregnant women and children), possess a (relatively) high barrier to resistance and exhibit minimal drug–drug interactions16. Virus tissue tropism further influences desirable drug properties. For example, infections involving the central nervous system require efficient blood–brain barrier penetration, whereas limited penetration may be preferable for peripheral viral infections. Consequently, distinct target product profiles may be required, even within a single viral genus. Within Ortho- flavivirus, for instance, West Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis virus Table 1 | RNA virus families covered in this Review Virus family Genome architecture Most relevant genera WHO Representative human pathogens Coronaviridae (+)ssRNA, non-segmented Alphacoronavirus Priority HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 Betacoronavirus SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, HCoV-OC43 Flaviviridae (+)ssRNA, non-segmented Hepacivirus Priority Hepatitis C virus Orthoflavivirus Dengue virus, yellow fever virus, West Nile virus, Zika virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, TBEV Togaviridae (+)ssRNA, non-segmented Alphavirus Priority Chikungunya virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, Eastern equine encephalitis virus Picornaviridae (+)ssRNA, non-segmented Enterovirus EV-A71, EV-D68, poliovirus, coxsackieviruses, rhinoviruses A–C Hepeviridae (+)ssRNA, non-segmented Paslahepevirus Hepatitis E virus Caliciviridae (+)ssRNA, non-segmented Norovirus Noroviruses Sapovirus Sapoviruses Filoviridae (−)ssRNA, non-segmented Orthoebolavirus Priority Ebola virus, Sudan virus Orthomarburgvirus Marburg virus Paramyxoviridae (−)ssRNA, non-segmented Morbillivirus Priority Measles virus, canine distemper virus Henipavirus Nipah virus, Hendra virus Respirovirus Human parainfluenza viruses 1 and 3 Orthorubulavirus Mumps virus, human parainfluenza viruses 2 and 4 Pneumoviridae (−)ssRNA, non-segmented Orthopneumovirus Respiratory syncytial virus Metapneumovirus Human metapneumovirus Arenaviridae (−)ssRNA, segmented Mammarenavirus Priority Lassa virus and LCMV (Old World); (−)ssRNA, negative-sense single-stranded RNA; EV, enterovirus; HCoV, human coronavirus; LCMV, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus; MERS, Middle East respiratory syndrome; SARS, severe acute respiratory syndrome; TBEV, tick-borne encephalitis virus. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article typically invade the central nerve system, whereas yellow fever virus and DENV do not17. The importance of preparedness against known viruses (such as EV-D6818, Ebola virus19, monkeypox virus20 and Andes hantavirus21) as well as against emerging viral threats (for example, SARS-CoV-2) has been repeatedly illustrated during outbreaks caused by these diverse viral pathogens. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19 pan- demic), no antiviral drugs were available at the onset. A stockpile of an oral, pan-family coronavirus BSA before the start of the COVID-19 pan- demic would likely have saved countless lives22,23. Remdesivir, originally discovered as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor of RSV24 and Ebola viruses25,26, was the only drug for which antiviral activity against coronaviruses had been systematically demonstrated in preclinical models before the pandemic27. In the absence of readily available and effective antiviral treat- ments, drug repurposing may need to be considered. Repurpos- ing can provide a rapid and relatively cost-effective response by leveraging de-risked drugs with existing preclinical and clinical safety data28,29. However, drugs developed or used for non-viral indi- cations are mostly unlikely to possess sufficient antiviral potency to curb outbreaks caused by newly emerging and (potentially highly) pathogenic viruses. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, extensive repurposing initiatives studied whether drugs approved for other indications could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication. Drugs such as azithro- mycin (antibiotic), itraconazole (antifungal), hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial, antirheumatic), niclosamide (anthelmintic), ivermectin (anthelmintic) and nitazoxanide (antiparasitic) rapidly entered numer- ous clinical trials, many of them small and underpowered, and even became, for some time, standard treatment in certain settings despite limited preclinical evidence30. Overall, drug repurposing efforts dur- ing the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic were largely unsuccessful, highlighting that such strategies should not be initiated only at the time a new virus emerges. A more realistic approach is to systematically assess existing drugs during epidemic or pandemic ‘peace-time’ against panels of viruses that are representative of high-risk families. Drugs with ‘reason- able’ in vitro activity can be further tested, alone or in combinations, in preclinical models13. Studies in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters revealed that combi- nations of two or three antivirals, each used at suboptimal or even inactive doses, can result in important antiviral effects31. To ration- ally develop combination strategies for BSAs, systematic preclinical testing of combinations across viral families is required. Extensive preclinical studies of the most promising combinations may help to guide strategies for stockpiling for epidemic or pandemic prepared- ness. The use of fixed-dose combinations (such as those used in the treatment of HIV infections) would be ideal. Yet, in outbreak situation with new pathogens, there will be insufficient time to develop such fixed-dose combinations; co-administration of individual drugs would therefore represent a more practical approach. Maximizing broader- spectrum activity while minimizing the risk of cross-resistance Box 2 | Examples of viral families with a positive-sense RNA genome and their clinical relevance Coronaviridae Viruses that cause a spectrum of respiratory illnesses, ranging from common cold (for example, human coronaviruses HCoV-229E, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-HKU1) to highly pathogenic zoonotic viruses, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV), Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) and SARS-CoV-2. Their broad host range, capacity for zoonotic spillover and ability to spread rapidly underscore the pandemic potential of this family and make them a key priority for preparedness. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on seasonal influenza viruses, specifically human influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria and B/Yamagata lineages. The central question is the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with an emphasis on creating drugs that can target multiple viral genera, families, or even cross families.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of antiviral agents active against RNA viruses, including approved and investigational drugs. It discusses the biological determinants underlying antiviral spectrum and outlines clinical development frameworks for evaluating such drugs, particularly in outbreak scenarios. The review does not report specific databases, search dates, or study counts.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that broader-spectrum antivirals are essential for addressing current unmet medical needs and for pandemic preparedness. It highlights the importance of developing drugs that can target multiple viral families or genera, as newly emerging viruses are likely to belong to known families. The review also emphasizes the need for a diversified portfolio of antivirals to combat RNA viruses effectively.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the term 'broad-spectrum' antiviral lacks a clear definition, and it proposes the term 'broader-spectrum' instead. It also identifies gaps in the development of antivirals for many RNA viruses, particularly those that are not part of the large commercial markets. Additionally, the review highlights the need for more research on the clinical development frameworks for BSAs, especially in the context of outbreaks.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that research should focus on identifying and validating new targets for broader-spectrum antivirals, particularly those that can act across multiple viral families or genera. It also recommends the development of antivirals for RNA viruses that currently lack effective treatments, such as certain influenza strains, and emphasizes the importance of accelerating clinical trials for these drugs during outbreaks.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with a focus on seasonal influenza viruses such as A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata. It highlights the need for such drugs to address current medical needs and enhance pandemic preparedness. The review discusses the rationale for BSAs, their biological determinants, and the clinical frameworks required for their evaluation. It also identifies controversies, such as the lack of a clear definition for 'broad-spectrum' antivirals, and evidence gaps in the development of antivirals for many RNA viruses. The implications emphasize the importance of research into new targets and the acceleration of clinical trials for BSAs during outbreaks.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本评论聚焦于季节性流感病毒,特别是人类流感病毒的甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、甲型H3N2流感病毒以及B/Victoria和B/Yamagata谱系。核心问题是开发针对RNA病毒的广谱直接作用抗病毒药物药物(BSAs),重点在于创建能够针对多种病毒属、科甚至跨科的药物。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本评论是对针对RNA病毒的抗病毒药物药物的系统分析,包括已批准和正在研究的药物。它讨论了抗病毒药物谱的生物学决定因素,并概述了评估此类药物的临床开发框架,特别是在暴发情境下。本评论未报告特定数据库、搜索日期或研究数量。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本评论得出结论,认为针对RNA病毒的广谱抗病毒药物药物对于解决当前未满足的医疗需求和加强大流行病应对能力至关重要。它强调了开发能够针对多种病毒科或属的药物的重要性,因为新出现的病毒很可能属于已知的病毒科。本评论还强调了需要针对RNA病毒开发多样化的抗病毒药物药物组合以有效应对这些病毒。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本评论指出,'广谱' 抗病毒药物这一术语缺乏明确的定义,并建议使用'更广谱'这一术语。它还指出了针对许多RNA病毒的抗病毒药物药物开发存在空白,尤其是那些不属于大型商业市场的病毒。此外,本评论强调了需要更多研究来完善BSAs的临床开发框架,特别是在暴发情境下。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 本评论建议研究应集中在识别和验证针对广谱抗病毒药物药物的新靶点,特别是那些能够作用于多种病毒科或属的靶点。它还推荐开发针对目前缺乏有效治疗的RNA病毒的抗病毒药物药物,例如某些流感毒株,并强调在暴发情境下加速这些药物的临床试验的重要性。

papers.title: Influenza A H1N1 Infection Triggers Endothelial Immunothrombosis via TNF-α–Tissue Factor–Thrombin Signaling in Human Brain Microvascular Endothelial Cells
papers.abstract: Severe Influenza A virus (IAV) infection is associated with endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and coagulation abnormalities. However, the mechanisms linking endothelial inflammatory activation to thrombosis remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether Influenza A/H1N1 induces an immunothrombotic phenotype in human brain microvascular endothelial cells. We infected HBEC-5i cells with Influenza A/H1N1 pdm09. We assessed viral infection by RT-qPCR detection of matrix (M) transcripts and by immunoblotting for the M1 protein. We evaluated endothelial responses by measuring TNF-α expression and secretion, Tissue Factor (TF) expression, TF-dependent factor Xa generation, and responses to recombinant TNF-α and thrombin. H1N1 infection increased TNF-α expression and secretion and enhanced TF expression and functional activity, indicating acquisition of a procoagulant endothelial phenotype. Recombinant TNF-α reproduced infection-associated TF induction, whereas thrombin enhanced TNF-α production and TF activity, supporting reciprocal amplification between inflammatory and coagulation pathways. These findings support a TNF-α–TF–thrombin feed-forward signaling circuit linking endothelial inflammation and coagulation during H1N1 infection. Influenza A/H1N1 induces an immunothrombotic phenotype in human brain microvascular endothelial cells, identifying this signaling axis as a potential mechanistic target for influenza-associated vascular and thrombotic complications.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 严重的流感A病毒(IAV)感染与内皮功能障碍、炎症和凝血异常有关。然而,将内皮炎症激活与血栓形成联系起来的机制仍不完全清楚。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们研究了流感A/H1N1是否在人类脑微血管内皮细胞中诱导免疫血栓表型。

elements_zh.main_results: H1N1 感染增加了 TNF-α 的表达和分泌,并增强了 TF 的表达和功能活性,表明获得了促凝血内皮表型。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现支持了一个TNF-α–TF–凝血酶的正反馈信号通路,将H1N1感染期间的内皮炎症与凝血联系起来。流感A/H1N1在人类脑微血管内皮细胞中诱导免疫血栓表型,这表明该信号轴可能是流感相关血管和血栓并发症的潜在机制靶点。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现对理解以及潜在靶向流感A/H1N1感染相关的血管和血栓并发症具有特定意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于使用了单一细胞系,并未探讨其在体内环境中的普遍性。证据强度为中等。

papers.abstract_zh: 严重甲型流感病毒 (IAV) 感染与内皮功能障碍、炎症和凝血异常有关。然而,内皮炎症激活与血栓形成之间的联系机制仍不完全清楚。我们研究了甲型 H1N1 流感是否会在人脑微血管内皮细胞中诱导免疫血栓表型。我们用甲型流感/H1N1 pdm09 感染 HBEC-5i 细胞。我们通过 RT-qPCR 检测基质 (M) 转录物和 M1 蛋白的免疫印迹来评估病毒感染。我们通过测量 TNF-α 表达和分泌、组织因子 (TF) 表达、TF 依赖性因子 Xa 生成以及对重组 TNF-α 和凝血酶的反应来评估内皮反应。H1N1 感染增加了 TNF-α 的表达和分泌,并增强了 TF 的表达和功能活性,表明获得了促凝血内皮表型。重组 TNF-α 再现了感染相关的 TF 诱导,而凝血酶增强了 TNF-α 的产生和 TF 活性,支持炎症和凝血途径之间的相互放大。这些发现支持 TNF-α-TF-凝血酶前馈信号回路在 H1N1 感染期间将内皮炎症和凝血联系起来。甲型 H1N1 流感在人脑微血管内皮细胞中诱导免疫血栓表型,将该信号轴确定为流感相关血管和血栓并发症的潜在机制靶点。

papers.title: Clinical Relevance of Multiplex PCR for Respiratory Pathogens in Hospitalized Adults with Influenza-Like Illness
papers.abstract: Objective: Influenza-like illness (ILI) is a major cause of hospitalization during respiratory virus seasons. This study aimed to investigate the pathogens detected in patients presenting with ILI symptoms and to analyze the results in conjunction with clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Materials and Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 446 hospitalized adults with ILI between epidemiological week 40 of 2024 and week 20 of 2025. Respiratory pathogens were identified using a multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay detecting 18 viral and 5 bacterial pathogens. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and radiological data were retrieved from electronic medical records. Disease severity was assessed using the CURB-65 score. Patients with Streptococcus pneumoniae detected by PCR were further evaluated according to radiological evidence of pneumonia. Results: At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 184/446 patients (41.2%), whereas no pathogen was identified in 262 patients (58.8%). The most frequently detected pathogens were S. pneumoniae, influenza viruses, and seasonal coronaviruses. The most common coinfection was influenza A plus S. Among patients with pneumococcal PCR positivity, those with radiologically confirmed pneumonia were significantly older, had higher CURB-65 scores, and more frequently had concomitant influenza infection than patients without radiological evidence of pneumonia. Conclusion: Multiplex molecular assays provide valuable information for respiratory pathogen detection, but molecular results, especially for bacterial pathogens such as S. pneumoniae, should be interpreted together with clinical and radiological findings.
papers.journal: Journal of Clinical Practice and Research

This study aimed to investigate the pathogens detected in patients presenting with ILI symptoms and to analyze the results in conjunction with clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective, single-center study included 446 hospitalized adults with ILI between epidemiological week 40 of 2024 and week 20 of 2025. The study focused on patients with ILI symptoms and included demographic, clinical, laboratory, and radiological data.
analysis.methods: Respiratory pathogens were identified using a multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay detecting 18 viral and 5 bacterial pathogens. Disease severity was assessed using the CURB-65 score. Patients with Streptococcus pneumoniae detected by PCR were further evaluated according to radiological evidence of pneumonia.
analysis.main_results: At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 184/446 patients (41.2%), whereas no pathogen was identified in 262 patients (58.8%). analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Multiplex molecular assays provide valuable information for respiratory pathogen detection, but molecular results, especially for bacterial pathogens such as S. pneumoniae, should be interpreted together with clinical and radiological findings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that multiplex PCR can enhance the detection of respiratory pathogens in hospitalized adults with ILI, which may improve diagnostic accuracy and guide appropriate clinical management.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was retrospective and single-center, which may limit its generalizability. The evidence is moderate as it is based on a single-center analysis and does not include long-term follow-up or comparative data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the pathogens detected in hospitalized adults with influenza-like illness (ILI) using a multiplex real-time PCR assay. The most frequent coinfection was influenza A and S. pneumoniae. The authors emphasized that molecular results should be interpreted alongside clinical and radiological findings. The study's findings suggest that multiplex PCR can improve diagnostic accuracy for respiratory pathogens in ILI patients, but its single-center design limits generalizability, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 流感样疾病(ILI)是呼吸道病毒季节住院的主要原因之一。本研究旨在调查出现ILI症状的患者中检测到的病原体,并结合临床、实验室和影像学检查结果进行分析。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究为回顾性单中心研究,纳入了2024年第40个流行病学周至2025年第20个流行病学周期间住院的446名成人患者。研究聚焦于具有ILI症状的患者,并包括人口学、临床、实验室和影像学数据。
elements_zh.methods: 使用一种多重实时聚合酶链反应(PCR)检测18种病毒和5种细菌病原体来识别呼吸道病原体。使用CURB-65评分评估疾病严重程度。对于PCR检测到的肺炎链球菌患者,根据影像学证据进一步评估肺炎情况。
elements_zh.main_results: 在446名患者中,至少检测到一种呼吸道病原体的有184例(41.2%),而未检测到任何病原体的有262例(58.8%)。最常检测到的病原体是肺炎链球菌、流感病毒和季节性冠状病毒。最常见的合并感染是甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09与肺炎链球菌。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 多重分子检测方法为呼吸道病原体检测提供了有价值的信息,但分子检测结果,尤其是细菌病原体如肺炎链球菌,应结合临床和影像学检查结果进行解释。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,多重PCR可以提高住院成人流感样疾病患者中呼吸道病原体的检出率,这可能有助于提高诊断准确性并指导适当的临床管理。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究为回顾性单中心研究,可能限制其普遍适用性。证据强度中等,因为它基于单中心分析,且未包括长期随访或比较数据。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Influenza-like illness (ILI) is a major cause of hospitalization during respiratory virus seasons. This study aimed to investigate the pathogens detected in patients presenting with ILI symptoms and to analyze the results in conjunction with clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This retrospective, single-center study included 446 hospitalized adults with ILI between epidemiological week 40 of 2024 and week 20 of 2025. The study focused on patients with ILI symptoms and included demographic, clinical, laboratory, and radiological data.
analysis_en.methods: Respiratory pathogens were identified using a multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay detecting 18 viral and 5 bacterial pathogens. Disease severity was assessed using the CURB-65 score. Patients with Streptococcus pneumoniae detected by PCR were further evaluated according to radiological evidence of pneumonia.
analysis_en.main_results: At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 184/446 patients (41.2%), whereas no pathogen was identified in 262 patients (58.8%). The most frequently detected pathogens were S. pneumoniae, influenza viruses, and seasonal coronaviruses. The most common coinfection was influenza A plus S.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: Multiplex molecular assays provide valuable information for respiratory pathogen detection, but molecular results, especially for bacterial pathogens such as S. pneumoniae, should be interpreted together with clinical and radiological findings.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that multiplex PCR can enhance the detection of respiratory pathogens in hospitalized adults with ILI, which may improve diagnostic accuracy and guide appropriate clinical management.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was retrospective and single-center, which may limit its generalizability. The evidence is moderate as it is based on a single-center analysis and does not include long-term follow-up or comparative data.

papers.title_zh: 住院成人流感样疾病中多重PCR对呼吸道病原体的临床意义
papers.source_body_en: Objective: Influenza-like illness (ILI) is a major cause of hospitalization during respiratory virus seasons. This study aimed to investigate the pathogens detected in patients presenting with ILI symptoms and to analyze the results in conjunction with clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Materials and Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 446 hospitalized adults with ILI between epidemiological week 40 of 2024 and week 20 of 2025. Respiratory pathogens were identified using a multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay detecting 18 viral and 5 bacterial pathogens. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and radiological data were retrieved from electronic medical records. Disease severity was assessed using the CURB-65 score. Patients with Streptococcus pneumoniae detected by PCR were further evaluated according to radiological evidence of pneumonia. Results: At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 184/446 patients (41.2%), whereas no pathogen was identified in 262 patients (58.8%). The most frequently detected pathogens were S. pneumoniae, influenza viruses, and seasonal coronaviruses. The most common coinfection was influenza A plus S. Among patients with pneumococcal PCR positivity, those with radiologically confirmed pneumonia were significantly older, had higher CURB-65 scores, and more frequently had concomitant influenza infection than patients without radiological evidence of pneumonia. Conclusion: Multiplex molecular assays provide valuable information for respiratory pathogen detection, but molecular results, especially for bacterial pathogens such as S. pneumoniae, should be interpreted together with clinical and radiological findings.
papers.abstract_zh: 目的:流感样疾病(ILI)是呼吸道病毒季节住院的主要原因之一。本研究旨在调查出现ILI症状的患者中检测到的病原体,并结合临床、实验室和影像学检查结果进行分析。方法:本研究为回顾性单中心研究,纳入了2024年第40个流行病学周至2025年第20个流行病学周期间住院的446名成人患者。使用一种多重实时聚合酶链反应(PCR)检测18种病毒和5种细菌病原体。从电子病历中提取了人口学、临床、实验室和影像学数据。使用CURB-65评分评估疾病严重程度。对于PCR检测到的肺炎链球菌患者,根据影像学证据进一步评估肺炎情况。结果:在446名患者中,至少检测到一种呼吸道病原体的有184例(41.2%),而未检测到任何病原体的有262例(58.8%)。最常检测到的病原体是肺炎链球菌、流感病毒和季节性冠状病毒。最常见的合并感染是甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09与肺炎链球菌。在PCR检测为肺炎链球菌阳性的患者中,影像学确认肺炎的患者显著更年长,CURB-65评分更高,并且更频繁地合并感染流感病毒。结论:多重分子检测方法为呼吸道病原体检测提供了有价值的信息,但分子检测结果,尤其是细菌病原体如肺炎链球菌,应结合临床和影像学检查结果进行解释。

papers.title: Parental Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Toward Influenza Vaccine Uptake Among Children in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: Seasonal influenza is a major public health concern, particularly among children who are at high risk of infection and can transmit the virus to others. Vaccination is the primary preventive measure. Parental knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) may influence vaccination decisions. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among Saudi parents attending primary healthcare centers in Jeddah. Parents with at least one child aged six months or older were eligible. Data were collected using a validated self-administered Arabic questionnaire assessing knowledge, attitudes, awareness, perceived barriers, and vaccine uptake. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used to examine associations, and binary logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of vaccine uptake. Results: A total of 308 parents participated. Influenza vaccine uptake was reported by 57.5% of participants. Nearly all participants (97.7%) demonstrated good knowledge, but the knowledge score was not significantly associated with vaccine uptake (p = 0.399). Parental attitude was a significant independent predictor (OR = 1.090, 95% CI: 1.033-1.149, p = 0.001). Education level was also significantly associated with uptake (p = 0.015), with lower-educated parents showing higher odds of vaccination compared to postgraduate-educated parents. Exposure to awareness campaigns was significantly associated with higher uptake (p < 0.001). The most reported barriers were the belief that vaccination was unnecessary (9.4%) and concerns about side effects (8.4%), both strongly associated with non-vaccination (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Although most parents had good knowledge about influenza vaccination, this did not translate into consistent vaccination behavior. Parental attitudes and awareness campaign exposure were the main predictors of vaccine uptake. Public health strategies should shift from broad factual dissemination to targeted, point-of-care counseling that addresses misconceptions about vaccine necessity and safety to improve influenza vaccination rates among children in Saudi Arabia.

papers.title: Editorial: Measuring vaccination perception, confidence, and uptake: advancing instrument development and validation
papers.abstract: Two contributions in this Research Topic directly advance the measurement science that motivated this Topic. ground the development of a new general measure of adult vaccine hesitancy for U.S. adults in the 3C framework, reporting content and face validity findings, including a content validity index derived from expert panel review, for an instrument intended to capture hesitancy across vaccine types rather than a single indication. report the development and psychometric evaluation of the Vaccine Hesitancy and Perception Scale toward COVID-19 vaccination (VHAPS-CV19), employing principal axis factoring with varimax rotation to derive a two-factor structure that distinguishes a hesitancy factor (confidence, complacency, and convenience) from a perception-and-trust factor (perceived benefit, barrier, susceptibility, severity, and trust), together with internal consistency estimates for each subscale. Together, the two studies trace the stages that valid measurement of a construct this complex demands, from item generation and content validity through factor structure and reliability testing, and they leave the field with two complementary tools, one general-purpose and one vaccine-specific, for future validation and cross-cultural adaptation work.Several contributions in this Topic examine hesitancy and uptake among healthcare workers, a population whose own vaccination behavior and patient communication directly shape public confidence. investigated uptake, willingness, and practices toward seasonal influenza vaccination among healthcare workers in China using a cross-sectional design. similarly employed a cross-sectional survey to explore attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccination among healthcare workers at a national infectious disease center in Singapore, while Aksoy et al. surveyed community pharmacists in Türkiye regarding their knowledge, attitudes, and barriers toward vaccination, extending the focus to frontline advocates outside the hospital setting. took a distinct, qualitative approach, interviewing healthcare workers at a London hospital to identify barriers and facilitators to measles vaccination uptake; this design complements the quantitative work elsewhere in the Topic, surfacing workplace, informational, and interpersonal factors that structured surveys tend to miss.A second cluster of contributions addresses hesitancy and uptake determinants in community and general-population samples, extending the scope of this Topic beyond influenza and COVID-19 to additional vaccine types and life stages. Rounding out the collection, Ali et al. provide a narrative review of enablers and barriers to influenza vaccine uptake among healthcare workers in Gulf Cooperation Council countries, synthesizing evidence from a regional context that is comparatively underrepresented in the vaccine hesitancy literature relative to North America, Europe, and East Asia. contribute a distinct but complementary perspective, presenting a multivariate analysis of risk factors for adverse events following rabies vaccination using real-world data. This work centers on vaccine safety rather than perception, but it is a reminder that confidence in vaccination rests on lived experience with tolerability as much as on attitudes and access, and that perception-focused instruments are best read alongside pharmacovigilance data.A few patterns stand out across this collection (Figure 1; Table 1). Geographically, contributions concentrate in China (six studies), with additional representation from the United States, Singapore, Türkiye, Vietnam, the United Kingdom, and the Gulf Cooperation Council region; populations in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America are absent, which limits how far these findings generalize and points to a direction for future Research Topics. Methodologically, most contributions rely on cross-sectional, self-report surveys. These designs are useful for generating hypotheses about correlates of hesitancy, but they cannot establish temporal precedence between attitude and behavior, and they remain vulnerable to social desirability and recall bias. Only one contribution employed qualitative interview methods, and none employed a longitudinal or experimental design; this concentration of designs mirrors the broader hesitancy literature and marks a gap that future work should close.Taken together, the contributions to this Research Topic make clear that vaccine decision-making has many layers. Hesitancy and confidence are shaped at once by individual psychology, professional role, cultural context, service accessibility, and direct experience with vaccine safety. The instrument development studies respond to a real methodological gap: the field needs measurement tools that are psychometrically sound and adaptable across populations. The determinant studies argue the opposite case for context. Findings from healthcare workers in the Gulf region, older adults in western China, and pharmacists in Türkiye are not interchangeable; each offers insight for the setting studied rather than a universal account of vaccine hesitancy.A few gaps remain for future research. Cross-cultural validation of the instruments introduced here, including measurement invariance testing and comparison against benchmarks such as the WHO SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale (2), would strengthen confidence in their applicability across populations. Longitudinal designs tracking how measured hesitancy or confidence relates to actual vaccination behavior over time, rather than to intention alone, would help close the well-documented gap between attitudinal measurement and uptake outcomes. Greater use of qualitative and mixed-methods designs, alongside the cross-sectional surveys predominant here, would help clarify mechanisms that quantitative models identify but cannot fully explain. Finally, as vaccine platforms and communication environments evolve, measurement tools will need periodic re-validation to remain sensitive to emerging determinants of hesitancy.

papers.title_original: Editorial: Measuring vaccination perception, confidence, and uptake: advancing instrument development and validation

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on seasonal influenza viruses, specifically human influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage. The central question is about measuring vaccination perception, confidence, and uptake, particularly in healthcare workers and other populations, to advance instrument development and validation.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on a collection of studies, primarily cross-sectional surveys, with one qualitative study. The evidence includes studies on seasonal influenza vaccination among healthcare workers in China, attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccination in Singapore, and knowledge, attitudes, and barriers toward vaccination among community pharmacists in Türkiye. The review does not explicitly report a meta-analysis or consensus process, but it synthesizes findings from multiple studies.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review highlights that vaccine hesitancy and confidence are influenced by individual psychology, professional role, cultural context, service accessibility, and direct experience with vaccine safety. It also emphasizes the need for psychometrically sound and adaptable measurement tools across populations.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a lack of studies in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, which limits the generalizability of findings. Additionally, it notes that most studies rely on cross-sectional designs, which cannot establish temporal precedence between attitude and behavior, and are vulnerable to social desirability and recall bias. There is also a need for longitudinal designs to better understand the relationship between measured hesitancy and actual vaccination behavior.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Future research should focus on cross-cultural validation of the instruments introduced, including measurement invariance testing and comparison against benchmarks such as the WHO SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale. Longitudinal designs tracking how measured hesitancy or confidence relates to actual vaccination behavior over time are also recommended.

analysis.summary_en: This editorial reviews the measurement science of vaccine hesitancy and confidence, particularly in the context of seasonal influenza viruses. It highlights the development of two complementary tools for assessing vaccine hesitancy: a general measure for U.S. adults and the Vaccine Hesitancy and Perception Scale toward COVID-19 vaccination (VHAPS-CV19). The review emphasizes the importance of psychometrically sound instruments and the need for cross-cultural validation. It also identifies methodological limitations, such as the reliance on cross-sectional designs and the absence of studies in certain regions, and suggests future research directions, including longitudinal studies and broader geographic representation.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点探讨了季节性流感病毒,特别是人类流感中的甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、甲型H3N2流感病毒和B/Victoria谱系。核心问题是关于测量疫苗接种的感知、信心和接受度,特别是在医疗工作者和其他人群中,以推进工具的开发和验证。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述基于一组研究,主要是横断面调查,包含一项定性研究。证据包括在中国医护人员中关于季节性流感和疫苗接种的研究,在新加坡关于对COVID-19 疫苗接种的态度的研究,以及在土耳其社区药房人员中关于疫苗接种的知识、态度和障碍的研究。该综述未明确报告进行荟萃分析或共识过程,但综合了多项研究的发现。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述强调,疫苗犹豫不决和信心受到个体心理、专业角色、文化背景、服务可及性以及直接接触疫苗安全性的经历的影响。它还强调需要在不同人群中使用心理测量学上可靠且可适应的测量工具。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 综述指出,在撒哈拉以南非洲、南亚和拉丁美洲缺乏相关研究,这限制了研究结果的普遍适用性。此外,它还指出大多数研究采用横断面设计,无法确定态度与行为之间的时间先后关系,并且容易受到社会可接受性偏差和回忆偏差的影响。还需要纵向研究设计,以更好地理解所测量的犹豫不决与实际行为之间的关系。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 未来的研究应侧重于对所引入工具的跨文化验证,包括测量不变性检验以及与世卫组织SAGE 疫苗犹豫量表等基准的比较。还建议采用纵向研究设计,追踪所测量的犹豫或信心如何随时间与实际疫苗接种行为相关联。

analysis_en.scope_and_question: The review focuses on seasonal influenza viruses, specifically human influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage. The central question is about measuring vaccination perception, confidence, and uptake, particularly in healthcare workers and other populations, to advance instrument development and validation.
analysis_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on a collection of studies, primarily cross-sectional surveys, with one qualitative study. The evidence includes studies on seasonal influenza vaccination among healthcare workers in China, attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccination in Singapore, and knowledge, attitudes, and barriers toward vaccination among community pharmacists in Türkiye. The review does not explicitly report a meta-analysis or consensus process, but it synthesizes findings from multiple studies.
analysis_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review highlights that vaccine hesitancy and confidence are influenced by individual psychology, professional role, cultural context, service accessibility, and direct experience with vaccine safety. It also emphasizes the need for psychometrically sound and adaptable measurement tools across populations.
analysis_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a lack of studies in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, which limits the generalizability of findings. Additionally, it notes that most studies rely on cross-sectional designs, which cannot establish temporal precedence between attitude and behavior, and are vulnerable to social desirability and recall bias. There is also a need for longitudinal designs to better understand the relationship between measured hesitancy and actual vaccination behavior.
analysis_en.research_and_practice_implications: Future research should focus on cross-cultural validation of the instruments introduced, including measurement invariance testing and comparison against benchmarks such as the WHO SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale. Longitudinal designs tracking how measured hesitancy or confidence relates to actual vaccination behavior over time are also recommended.

papers.title_zh: 编者按:测量疫苗接种感知、信心和采纳:推进工具开发与验证
papers.source_body_en: Two contributions in this Research Topic directly advance the measurement science that motivated this Topic. ground the development of a new general measure of adult vaccine hesitancy for U.S. adults in the 3C framework, reporting content and face validity findings, including a content validity index derived from expert panel review, for an instrument intended to capture hesitancy across vaccine types rather than a single indication. report the development and psychometric evaluation of the Vaccine Hesitancy and Perception Scale toward COVID-19 vaccination (VHAPS-CV19), employing principal axis factoring with varimax rotation to derive a two-factor structure that distinguishes a hesitancy factor (confidence, complacency, and convenience) from a perception-and-trust factor (perceived benefit, barrier, susceptibility, severity, and trust), together with internal consistency estimates for each subscale. Together, the two studies trace the stages that valid measurement of a construct this complex demands, from item generation and content validity through factor structure and reliability testing, and they leave the field with two complementary tools, one general-purpose and one vaccine-specific, for future validation and cross-cultural adaptation work.Several contributions in this Topic examine hesitancy and uptake among healthcare workers, a population whose own vaccination behavior and patient communication directly shape public confidence. investigated uptake, willingness, and practices toward seasonal influenza vaccination among healthcare workers in China using a cross-sectional design. similarly employed a cross-sectional survey to explore attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccination among healthcare workers at a national infectious disease center in Singapore, while Aksoy et al. surveyed community pharmacists in Türkiye regarding their knowledge, attitudes, and barriers toward vaccination, extending the focus to frontline advocates outside the hospital setting. took a distinct, qualitative approach, interviewing healthcare workers at a London hospital to identify barriers and facilitators to measles vaccination uptake; this design complements the quantitative work elsewhere in the Topic, surfacing workplace, informational, and interpersonal factors that structured surveys tend to miss.A second cluster of contributions addresses hesitancy and uptake determinants in community and general-population samples, extending the scope of this Topic beyond influenza and COVID-19 to additional vaccine types and life stages. Rounding out the collection, Ali et al. provide a narrative review of enablers and barriers to influenza vaccine uptake among healthcare workers in Gulf Cooperation Council countries, synthesizing evidence from a regional context that is comparatively underrepresented in the vaccine hesitancy literature relative to North America, Europe, and East Asia. contribute a distinct but complementary perspective, presenting a multivariate analysis of risk factors for adverse events following rabies vaccination using real-world data. This work centers on vaccine safety rather than perception, but it is a reminder that confidence in vaccination rests on lived experience with tolerability as much as on attitudes and access, and that perception-focused instruments are best read alongside pharmacovigilance data.A few patterns stand out across this collection (Figure 1; Table 1). Geographically, contributions concentrate in China (six studies), with additional representation from the United States, Singapore, Türkiye, Vietnam, the United Kingdom, and the Gulf Cooperation Council region; populations in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America are absent, which limits how far these findings generalize and points to a direction for future Research Topics. Methodologically, most contributions rely on cross-sectional, self-report surveys. These designs are useful for generating hypotheses about correlates of hesitancy, but they cannot establish temporal precedence between attitude and behavior, and they remain vulnerable to social desirability and recall bias. Only one contribution employed qualitative interview methods, and none employed a longitudinal or experimental design; this concentration of designs mirrors the broader hesitancy literature and marks a gap that future work should close.Taken together, the contributions to this Research Topic make clear that vaccine decision-making has many layers. Hesitancy and confidence are shaped at once by individual psychology, professional role, cultural context, service accessibility, and direct experience with vaccine safety. The instrument development studies respond to a real methodological gap: the field needs measurement tools that are psychometrically sound and adaptable across populations. The determinant studies argue the opposite case for context. Findings from healthcare workers in the Gulf region, older adults in western China, and pharmacists in Türkiye are not interchangeable; each offers insight for the setting studied rather than a universal account of vaccine hesitancy.A few gaps remain for future research. Cross-cultural validation of the instruments introduced here, including measurement invariance testing and comparison against benchmarks such as the WHO SAGE Vaccine Hesitancy Scale (2), would strengthen confidence in their applicability across populations. Longitudinal designs tracking how measured hesitancy or confidence relates to actual vaccination behavior over time, rather than to intention alone, would help close the well-documented gap between attitudinal measurement and uptake outcomes. Greater use of qualitative and mixed-methods designs, alongside the cross-sectional surveys predominant here, would help clarify mechanisms that quantitative models identify but cannot fully explain. Finally, as vaccine platforms and communication environments evolve, measurement tools will need periodic re-validation to remain sensitive to emerging determinants of hesitancy.

papers.title: Influenza vaccination in childhood and adolescence. Evaluation of the 2025-2026 campaign in Spain and improvement strategies. Report by AEV, CAV-AEP and SEIP.
papers.abstract: Seasonal influenza represents a significant burden in childhood. This article analyzes pediatric influenza vaccination during the 2025-2026 campaign, as well as epidemiological, effectiveness, and preliminary vaccination coverage data. Routine vaccination against influenza between ages 6 and 59 months, as well as the extension of the recommendation up to 17 years, as outlined in the 2025 AEV, CAV-AEP, and SEIP consensus document, is key to individual and collective protection. We propose advancing further in developing effective strategies to continue increasing vaccination coverage, as well as expanding the age range for vaccination, as has already been implemented in some autonomous communities in 2025-2026.

papers.full_text: AbstractBackgroundContinuous monitoring of both influenza vaccine protection and behavioural determinants of infection is important for understanding related risks. Evidence on influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) in China during the 2024–2025 season, however, remains limited. We aimed to assess influenza VE among healthcare-seeking outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) and to examine the contact patterns associated with infection risk.MethodsWe enrolled 928 outpatients with ILI from three sentinel hospitals in Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China, between December 2024 and March 2025 in a test-negative case-control study. We confirmed influenza infection using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and collected vaccination history and social contact frequency and duration through questionnaires. We estimated VE using logistic regression with covariate adjustment, and otherwise analysed social contact patterns and performed exploratory sequencing of six randomly selected influenza-positive samples.ResultsOur full sample comprised 928 participants. We excluded 21 infants younger than 6 months from the VE analysis and included 907 participants, of whom 121 tested positive and 786 tested negative. The overall adjusted VE against medically attended influenza was 42.3% (95% credible interval = 11.1–62.5). In the analysis of social contacts for all 928 participants, test-positive children aged 0–10 years and adults aged 65 years or older reported more frequent and longer social contact than their test-negative counterparts. Exploratory sequencing of six samples suggested no major antigenic mismatch with the vaccine strains, but the very small number of sequenced samples limits the generalisability of this finding.ConclusionsInfluenza vaccination provided moderate protection against medically attended influenza, while contact patterns were associated with infection risk among children and older adults. Combined vaccination and behavioural interventions warrant further evaluation, as the observational design of this study and its use of self-reporting data limit causal inference.Keywords : influenza, influenza vaccination, vaccine effectiveness, test-negative design, contact patterns, China METHODSSetting and study designWe conducted a multicentre test-negative case-control study from 8 December 2024 (epidemiological week 50) to 30 March 2025 (epidemiological week 13) among outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) from three sentinel hospitals in Yining and Horgos, Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China. These sentinel outpatient clinics serve as the core data source for the national influenza surveillance network and support the systematic collection of epidemiological and virological data.In accordance with the Chinese National Influenza Surveillance Protocol, we defined ILI as the presence of fever (body temperature ≥38°C) accompanied by a cough or sore throat [33]. We randomly selected 10–40 patients (typically 20) with ILI each week from whom we collected nasal or nasopharyngeal specimens for influenza testing using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), and administered a structured questionnaire to collect demographic information, influenza vaccination history, and social contact patterns. Trained hospital staff administered structured questionnaires and recorded the responses in an electronic database. We linked the questionnaire records to the corresponding laboratory results using unique study identifiers.We included outpatients who presented with ILI at a sentinel hospital, understood the questionnaire, and provided verbal informed consent, either personally or through a guardian. We excluded participants younger than six months of age from the VE analysis because maternal antibodies could provide protection. We truncated the number of reported daily contact counts above 30 at 30 in the contact analysis to reduce the influence of outliers.Outcome variableWe defined the influenza test result as a dichotomous variable, categorised as positive or negative based on RT-PCR analysis of nasopharyngeal swab specimens. We performed testing using the Zhuocheng Huisheng Influenza A/B Duplex real-time PCR detection kit (Beijing Zhuocheng Huisheng Bioscience Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). This kit used specific primers and fluorescent probes targeting influenza A and B viruses and included an internal control that monitors the entire process from nucleic acid extraction to amplification, thereby reducing the risk of false-negative results.Exposure variablesWe defined influenza vaccination status as the primary exposure variable based on data reported by the participants or their guardians. We classified participants as vaccinated if they had received at least one dose of a seasonal influenza vaccine, including egg-based, cell-based, trivalent, and quadrivalent vaccines, within the past 24 months, with the most recent dose being administered at least 14 days before symptom onset. We classified participants who did not meet these criteria as unvaccinated.We defined social contact pattern as the secondary exposure variable and characterised it by contact frequency and duration according to the POLYMOD study criteria [22]. We defined conversational contact as a face-to-face conversation with an exchange of at least three words, and physical contact as any skin-to-skin interaction, such as handshaking, hugging, or kissing.CovariatesWe collected potential confounders using structured questionnaires (Text S1 in the Online Supplementary Document), including demographic characteristics such as age, sex, and ethnicity; clinical and behavioural characteristics, such as baseline health conditions, health-related behaviours, and daily habits; and temporal variables, such as the dates of symptom onset and visit dates. We grouped age for further analysis and used symptom onset and visit dates to derive the epidemiological week for adjustment for long-term and seasonal trends.Viral sequencing sample selection and reference sequencesThe national Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) influenza surveillance protocol requires sentinel hospitals to perform viral genetic sequencing on a subset of influenza-positive samples during routine surveillance to monitor genetic variation among circulating strains, rather than sequencing all positive samples [33]. We selected 6 out of 121 influenza-positive samples for exploratory sequencing in accordance with this protocol.We retrieved global influenza A(H1N1) reference sequences from the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID) database [34]. We selected 170 sequences containing both haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) gene segments and combined them with six viral isolates obtained in this study.Statistical analysisWe used a Bayesian logistic regression model adjusted for covariates to estimate VE. We specified an informative prior for the vaccination coefficient, centred on a VE of 40% based on historical CDC estimates [35]. We calculated VE for laboratory-confirmed influenza as (1 − odds ratio) × 100% and expressed uncertainty in the model coefficients using 95% credible intervals (CrIs) derived from the posterior distribution.We performed targeted sequencing of 6 virus isolates from influenza-positive participants and conducted phylogenetic analysis together with 170 reference sequences retrieved from GISAID. We aligned the sequences using ClustalW in Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis, version 12 [36] and assessed alignment quality using ESPript [37]. We constructed a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree using IQ-TREE [38]. We then compared sequences within a specific monophyletic clade to identify variable sites and non-synonymous mutations (Text S3 in the Online Supplementary Document).We performed age standardisation according to the 2020 China Population Census. We used linear regression to quantify age-specific differences in contact frequency and duration (β) between influenza test-positive and test-negative participants. We smoothed the contact matrices using Gaussian kernel density estimation. We used stratified χ2 tests to compare the distributions of contact setting, frequency, and duration between the groups. We used a Bayesian negative binomial regression model to assess the effects of demographic characteristics and contact setting and evaluated model robustness against a gamma model (Text S4 in the Online Supplementary Document).We conducted subgroup analyses for VE by age group (6 months to 6 years, 7–17 years, 18–59 years, and ≥60 years) and influenza subtype (A(H1), A(H3), and B/Victoria). We performed similar analyses for social contacts by age groups (0–5 years, 6–15 years, 16–65 years, and >65 years) based on immune status, social behaviours, and health risks, with further stratification by sex (male and female), household size (small, ≤3 persons; medium, 4 persons; large, ≥5 persons), and contact setting (home, school, workplace, leisure, and other) (Text S4 in the Online Supplementary Document).We also conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of the VE estimates and social contact analyses (Text S5 in the Online Supplementary Document). For the VE analysis, we assessed the effects of including infants younger than six months, treating age and body mass index as continuous variables, and adjusting for the symptom onset date. For the social contact analysis, we restricted the sample to unvaccinated participants to reduce potential confounding by vaccination status.We performed all statistical analyses and phylogenetic tree visualisations using R, version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria), with the ‘EBImage’, ‘seqinr’, ‘ape’, ‘phytools’, ‘ggplot2’, ‘treeio’, and ‘ggtree’ packages. Setting and study designWe conducted a multicentre test-negative case-control study from 8 December 2024 (epidemiological week 50) to 30 March 2025 (epidemiological week 13) among outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) from three sentinel hospitals in Yining and Horgos, Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China. These sentinel outpatient clinics serve as the core data source for the national influenza surveillance network and support the systematic collection of epidemiological and virological data.In accordance with the Chinese National Influenza Surveillance Protocol, we defined ILI as the presence of fever (body temperature ≥38°C) accompanied by a cough or sore throat [33]. We randomly selected 10–40 patients (typically 20) with ILI each week from whom we collected nasal or nasopharyngeal specimens for influenza testing using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), and administered a structured questionnaire to collect demographic information, influenza vaccination history, and social contact patterns. Trained hospital staff administered structured questionnaires and recorded the responses in an electronic database. We linked the questionnaire records to the corresponding laboratory results using unique study identifiers.We included outpatients who presented with ILI at a sentinel hospital, understood the questionnaire, and provided verbal informed consent, either personally or through a guardian. We excluded participants younger than six months of age from the VE analysis because maternal antibodies could provide protection. We truncated the number of reported daily contact counts above 30 at 30 in the contact analysis to reduce the influence of outliers. Additional material Online Supplementary Document Supplementary Materials Online Supplementary Document RESULTSWe enrolled 928 participants with ILI between 8 December 2024 and 30 March 2025. For the VE analysis, we excluded 21 infants younger than 6 months and included 907 participants, of whom 121 (13.3%) tested positive for influenza: 101 (83.5%) had influenza A and 20 (16.5%) had influenza B (Table 1).
