The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. Pediatric respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Throughout the study period, the data-collecting hospital, clinical laboratory, and respiratory pathogen testing framework remained consistent. Annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient volumes from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from hospital administrative records and used to calculate the number of respiratory pathogen testing records per 100 inpatient admissions as a contextual measure of testing volume across study periods.2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The overall study design, data-cleaning process, 7-day deduplication procedure, study-period classification, and analytical workflow are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Study design, data cleaning, and analytical workflow. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. NPI, non-pharmaceutical intervention.Flowchart of study record selection and analysis. A total of 21,132 pediatric 13-pathogen respiratory nucleic acid testing records were screened; 836 records were excluded during data cleaning, leaving 20,296 preliminary records. After excluding 46 non-first repeat tests within 7 days, 20,250 records remained. These were classified into the NPI period (January 2021-December 2022; n = 6,490) and post-NPI period (January 2023–December 2025; n = 13,760), followed by risk-ratio, interrupted time-series, multivariable, age-stratified, co-detection, and sensitivity analyses.Children were categorized into four age groups: <1, 1–<3, 3–<6, and 6–14 years. This age stratification was selected according to commonly used pediatric respiratory infection epidemiology and the social contact patterns of children in China, broadly corresponding to infancy, early childhood mainly under home care, kindergarten age, and school age.2.3Respiratory pathogen testing and pathogen definitionsRespiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was performed using a multiplex detection kit for 13 respiratory pathogens based on fluorescence PCR followed by capillary electrophoresis (PN: 1060071; Health GeneTech Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China). Nucleic acid extraction was performed using a TANBead SLA-32 automated nucleic acid extraction system. PCR amplification was performed using a SLAN-96P real-time PCR system. Amplification products were detected using an Applied Biosystems 3500 Dx Genetic Analyzer for capillary electrophoresis-based detection and fragment analysis. Sample processing, nucleic acid extraction, PCR amplification, capillary electrophoresis, quality control, and result interpretation were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and local standard operating procedures.The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories: influenza A virus not further classified by this panel (InfA-NFC), influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus, influenza B virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human rhinovirus, human adenovirus, seasonal human coronaviruses, human bocavirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia spp. In this study, InfA-NFC referred to records positive for the manufacturer-reported generic influenza A target, listed as InfA in the manufacturer's instructions, but not classified as influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus or seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus. The seasonal human coronaviruses category did not include SARS-CoV-2. Throughout the study period, SARS-CoV-2 testing, when clinically indicated, was performed through a separate dedicated nucleic acid testing pathway and was therefore not included in the fixed 13-target respiratory pathogen panel analyzed in this study. The Chlamydia category was not further differentiated into C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae. Pathogen abbreviations, full pathogen names, manufacturer-reported detection targets, and limits of detection are provided in Supplementary Table S1.A composite influenza A variable was defined as positivity for any influenza A-related analytic category, including InfA-NFC, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, or seasonal influenza A(H3N2) virus. This composite variable was used only for descriptive summaries and was not included as an additional category in the main risk ratio, multiple-comparison, interrupted time-series, or multivariable regression analyses to avoid double counting. Overall positivity was defined as positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Co-detection was defined as positivity for two or more of the 13 main pathogen categories in the same testing record. Positivity and co-detection rates were calculated using the corresponding number of testing records as the denominator. A 13-target-negative record was defined as a testing record in which none of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was detected. Overall positivity and 13-target-negative proportions describe laboratory detection among tested pediatric and neonatal inpatients and were not intended as estimates of community incidence or prevalence.2.4Study periods, seasons, and school-term statusThe study period was divided according to the timing of COVID-19 policy adjustment in China and the monthly structure of the dataset. January 2021 to December 2022 was defined as the NPI period, and January 2023 to December 2025 was defined as the post-NPI period. In interrupted time-series analyses, January 2023 was treated as the first post-intervention month. Seasons were defined by calendar month: spring, March to May; summer, June to August; autumn, September to November; and winter, December to February. School-term status was defined at the calendar-day level according to the official local school calendar rather than by calendar month alone and assigned to each testing record based on the application date. Each testing record was classified as occurring during an in-school term or a vacation period. This variable was used as a population-level contextual indicator of periods with increased or decreased community contact networks related to kindergarten and school attendance.2.5Meteorological and air-quality dataDaily meteorological observations for Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China were obtained from RP5 (Reliable Prognosis), a publicly available weather data platform providing observational data from ground weather stations. Daily air quality index (AQI) records were obtained from the 2345 Weather historical weather database for Nanchong, a publicly accessible weather and air-quality information platform that provides city-level historical weather records with daily air-quality information (https://tianqi.2345.com/wea_history/57411.htm; accessed July 4, 2026). Before monthly aggregation, extracted AQI records were checked for completeness, date consistency, plausible value ranges, and temporal continuity. Daily temperature, relative humidity, and AQI records were aggregated into monthly means for each calendar month and linked to individual testing records by year-month. Temperature was modeled per 1 °C increase, relative humidity per 10% increase, and AQI per 10-unit increase. Meteorological and AQI variables were available for all 60 calendar months from January 2021 to December 2025 and were matched to the testing dataset by year-month.2.6Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were based on the final analytic dataset of 20,250 testing records. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges or means with standard deviations, as appropriate. All tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons across the 13 main pathogen categories, the Benjamini–Hochberg method was used to control the false discovery rate (FDR). All statistical analyses were performed using Python software. Data management and aggregation were conducted using pandas and NumPy. Statistical calculations and modeling were performed using SciPy and statsmodels, and figures were generated using matplotlib.2.6.1Baseline characteristics and period comparisonsBaseline characteristics and pathogen detection profiles were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Categorical variables were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test or t test, depending on distributional characteristics. The composite influenza A variable was presented only as a descriptive summary, with influenza A subtypes listed separately. Continuous age is presented as median (interquartile range) and was compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods using the Mann–Whitney U test.2.6.2Risk ratio analysisDetection risks for the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. For each pathogen, positivity rates were calculated for both periods, and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. FDR-adjusted P values were used to assess statistical robustness under multiple testing. As an additional RSV-focused supplementary analysis, age was reclassified into clinically relevant categories for RSV burden and prevention strategies. RSV detection was first compared between children aged <2 years and those aged ≥2 years. Children were further categorized as 0–<6 months, 6–<12 months, 12–<24 months, and ≥24 months. For each category, RSV positivity was summarized for the NPI and post-NPI periods, and post-NPI vs. NPI risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), P values, and FDR-adjusted P values were calculated. This RSV-specific supplementary analysis was designed to provide clinical and public-health detail for the age windows most relevant to infant and toddler RSV prevention.2.6.3Interrupted time-series analysisTo evaluate whether the period difference in overall positivity could reflect a general long-term trend, monthly overall positivity was first analyzed using a single time-trend model without an interruption term. A segmented interrupted time-series model was then fitted using January 2023 as the first post-interruption month, corresponding to the January 8, 2023 policy transition, to estimate the pre-interruption trend, immediate level change, and post-interruption trend change. A joint Wald test evaluated the combined evidence for the immediate level and trend changes, and a grouped binomial model based on monthly positive and negative counts was used as a sensitivity analysis.Interrupted time-series (ITS) segmented regression models were used to assess immediate level changes and post-intervention trend changes in monthly pathogen positivity after the lifting of NPIs. ITS and segmented regression models are commonly used to evaluate level and slope changes after public health policy or intervention changes (21–24).For each pathogen, the monthly positivity rate was used as the outcome. The core independent variables included time, intervention status, and time after intervention. Month fixed effects were included to account for seasonality. Models were weighted by the monthly number of testing records. Newey–West robust standard errors were used to account for potential autocorrelation (25). The primary model used Newey–West lag = 1, and lag = 3 was used as a sensitivity analysis.The model was specified as: Yt = β0 + β1 × time + β2 × intervention + β3 × post-intervention time + month fixed effects + εt, where β1 represents the pre-intervention monthly trend, β2 represents the immediate level change after the lifting of NPIs, and β3 represents the post-intervention trend change.2.6.4Multivariable logistic regressionTo evaluate factors associated with pathogen positivity, separate multivariable logistic regression models were fitted for each of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. The core independent variables were monthly mean temperature, monthly mean relative humidity, monthly mean AQI, and school-term status. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, and pandemic phase. Because meteorological exposures, seasonality, and time trends may be correlated, season was not included in the primary model to reduce potential collinearity; this approach was consistent with general considerations in environmental time-series modeling (26). Cluster-robust standard errors were estimated at the year-month level. Results were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% CIs. To assess whether environmental and temporal associations differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods, separate interaction models were fitted by adding temperature × phase, relative humidity × phase, AQI × phase, and school term × phase terms to the pathogen-specific multivariable models. Across 13 pathogen categories and four contextual factors, 52 interaction tests were prespecified. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025. After 7-day deduplication within the same child, 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included. The NPI period was January 2021–December 2022, and the post-NPI period was January 2023–December 2025. Thirteen pathogen categories were analyzed using period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status.ResultsOverall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher in the post-NPI period (15.2% vs. 6.0%). Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed heterogeneous patterns: human adenovirus showed a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005), whereas human rhinovirus showed a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of human respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context.

full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Study population and baseline characteristicsA total of 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included in the main analysis, covering 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025, including 6,490 records during the NPI period and 13,760 during the post-NPI period. Monthly testing volume and overall positivity trends are shown in Figure 2. Among the included records, 11,191 were from boys (55.3%) and 9,059 from girls (44.7%). The median age was 2.00 years overall and in both the NPI and post-NPI periods. The overall IQR was 0.75–4.00 years, while the IQRs were 0.67–4.00 years during the NPI period and 0.75–4.00 years during the post-NPI period. The largest age group was 3–<6 years (30.2%), followed by <1 year (29.4%), 1–<3 years (25.3%), and 6–14 years (15.1%). Overall, 16,871 records (83.3%) were collected during school terms and 3,379 (16.7%) during vacation periods. Baseline demographic and temporal characteristics differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods, including sex distribution, age group, season, and school-term status (Table 1).Figure 2Monthly testing volume and overall respiratory pathogen positivity from January 2021 to December 2025. The grey bars show the monthly number of pediatric respiratory pathogen testing records, and the red line shows the overall positivity rate for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. The vertical dashed line indicates the start of the post-NPI period in January 2023. NPI, non-pharmaceutical intervention.Combined bar-and-line chart showing monthly pediatric respiratory pathogen testing volume and overall positivity from January 2021 to December 2025. Gray bars represent the number of testing records in each month, and the red line represents the percentage positive for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Both measures fluctuate over time. A vertical dashed line at January 2023 marks the start of the post-NPI period, separating the January 2021–December 2022 NPI period from the January 2023–December 2025 post-NPI period.Table 1Baseline characteristics and respiratory pathogen detection profiles of pediatric testing records during the NPI and post-NPI periods.CharacteristicOverall (N = 20,250)NPI period (N = 6,490)Post-NPI period (N = 13,760)P valueAge, years, median (IQR)2.00 (0.75–4.00)2.00 (0.67–4.00)2.00 (0.75–4.00)<0.001Sex0.013 Male11,191 (55.3)3,669 (56.5)7,522 (54.7) Female9,059 (44.7)2,821 (43.5)6,238 (45.3)Age group<0.001 <1 year5,961 (29.4)2,058 (31.7)3,903 (28.4) 1–<3 years5,115 (25.3)1,751 (27.0)3,364 (24.4) 3–<6 years6,112 (30.2)1,877 (28.9)4,235 (30.8) 6–14 years3,062 (15.1)804 (12.4)2,258 (16.4)Season<0.001 Spring5,608 (27.7)1,860 (28.7)3,748 (27.2) Summer3,708 (18.3)1,453 (22.4)2,255 (16.4) Autumn4,124 (20.4)1,007 (15.5)3,117 (22.7) Winter6,810 (33.6)2,170 (33.4)4,640 (33.7)School-term status<0.001 Vacation3,379 (16.7)1,389 (21.4)1,990 (14.5) In-school term16,871 (83.3)5,101 (78.6)11,770 (85.5)Overall detection indicatorsOverall positivity14,191 (70.1)3,813 (58.8)10,378 (75.4)<0.001Co-detection2,477 (12.2)391 (6.0)2,086 (15.2)<0.001Composite influenza A1,433 (7.1)122 (1.9)1,311 (9.5)<0.001Pathogen-specific positivityInfA-NFC187 (0.9)8 (0.1)179 (1.3)<0.00109H1552 (2.7)1 (0.0)551 (4.0)<0.001H3695 (3.4)113 (1.7)582 (4.2)<0.001HPIV1,547 (7.6)298 (4.6)1,249 (9.1)<0.001HMPV1,669 (8.2)402 (6.2)1,267 (9.2)<0.001Mp1,884 (9.3)386 (5.9)1,498 (10.9)<0.001HRSV3,084 (15.2)812 (12.5)2,272 (16.5)<0.001HADV1,242 (6.1)476 (7.3)766 (5.6)<0.001HRV4,859 (24.0)1,404 (21.6)3,455 (25.1)<0.001Boca299 (1.5)76 (1.2)223 (1.6)0.016Ch153 (0.8)39 (0.6)114 (0.8)0.097InfB432 (2.1)162 (2.5)270 (2.0)0.016HCOV284 (1.4)43 (0.7)241 (1.8)<0.001Data are shown as n (%) unless otherwise indicated. Continuous age is presented as median (interquartile range) and was compared using the Mann–Whitney U test.Mean annual testing volume was 3,245.0 records during the NPI period and 4,586.7 during the post-NPI period, representing a 41.3% increase. Over the same periods, mean annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient admissions increased from 7,362.0 to 8,275.7, representing a 12.4% increase. The number of testing records per 100 inpatient admissions increased from 44.08 to 55.42, a relative increase of 25.7% (Supplementary Table S2).3.2Overall positivity and pathogen detection profileOverall positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was 70.1% (14,191/20,250). The overall positivity rate increased from 58.8% (3,813/6,490) during the NPI period to 75.4% (10,378/13,760) during the post-NPI period (P < 0.001). Co-detection of two or more pathogen categories was observed in 12.2% of records overall and increased from 6.0% (391/6,490) to 15.2% (2,086/13,760) after the lifting of NPIs (P < 0.001). Human rhinovirus was the most frequently detected pathogen category 24.0% (4,859/20,250), followed by human respiratory syncytial virus 15.2% (3,084/20,250), Mycoplasma pneumoniae 9.3% (1,884/20,250), human metapneumovirus 8.2% (1,669/20,250), human parainfluenza virus 7.6% (1,547/20,250), and human adenovirus 6.1% (1,242/20,250). The composite influenza A variable was positive in 7.1% of records, but it was used only for descriptive purposes and was not included as an additional category in the main 13-pathogen analyses. Overall, 29.9% (6,059/20,250) of testing records were negative for all 13 main pathogen categories, including 41.2% (2,677/6,490) during the NPI period and 24.6% (3,382/13,760) during the post-NPI period.In the RSV-focused age-stratified supplementary analysis, children younger than 2 years accounted for 1,854 of 3,084 RSV-positive records (60.1%). Overall RSV positivity was higher among children aged <2 years than among those aged ≥2 years (21.0% vs. 10.8%; RR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.82–2.08; P < 0.001). This excess was observed in both the NPI period (18.7% vs. 7.1%; RR, 2.63; 95% CI, 2.28–3.03; P < 0.001) and the post-NPI period (22.2% vs. 12.4%; RR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.66–1.93; P < 0.001). In finer age categories, overall RSV positivity was 19.7% in children aged 0–<6 months, 23.1% in those aged 6–<12 months, 21.1% in those aged 12–<24 months, and 10.8% in those aged ≥24 months. Period-specific comparisons are provided in Supplementary Table S3.3.3Changes in pathogen detection risks between periodsCompared with the NPI period, the post-NPI period showed increased detection risks for most pathogen categories after false discovery rate correction (Table 2). Human respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, and human bocavirus also showed significant increases after the lifting of NPIs, with RRs of 1.32 (95% CI, 1.22–1.42), 1.16 (95% CI, 1.10–1.23), and 1.38 (95% CI, 1.07–1.79), respectively. full_text_sections.discussion: 4Discussion4.1Principal findingsThis 5-year hospital-based laboratory surveillance study identified marked changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with distinct temporal patterns across pathogens. Overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also more frequent (15.2% vs. 6.0%). At the aggregate level, overall positivity showed a significant long-term increasing trend over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis using January 2023 as the interruption point showed no statistically significant immediate level or slope change. At the pathogen-specific level, ITS analyses revealed distinct temporal trajectories across pathogens, with human adenovirus showing a robust immediate decrease and human rhinovirus showing a significant positive trend change and a positive post-NPI slope. Associations with environmental factors and school-calendar status were likewise pathogen-specific, and phase-interaction analyses further showed that selected associations with temperature, relative humidity, and school-term status differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Overall, these findings demonstrate a complex temporal profile of pediatric respiratory pathogen detection characterized by a long-term aggregate trend, pathogen-specific changes, and associations with environmental and school-calendar factors.4.2Overall positivity, long-term trend, and co-detection across study periodsCOVID-19-related NPIs substantially altered the circulation of common respiratory pathogens (7–11), and subsequent studies reported renewed circulation and altered epidemiological patterns of multiple respiratory pathogens following relaxation of these measures (12–16). In our study, overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period. Further analysis of the overall temporal trend showed that overall positivity increased by an average of 0.49 percentage points per month over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis with January 2023 as the interruption point did not show significant changes in the overall level or trend. These findings place the higher overall positivity observed in the post-NPI period within a broader long-term upward trend and suggest that aggregate measures may not fully capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics across individual pathogens.Co-detection also increased markedly in the post-NPI period, and this increase was supported by both the period comparison and weighted ITS analysis. This pattern may reflect greater temporal overlap in the circulation of multiple respiratory pathogens, thereby increasing the likelihood of detecting more than one pathogen in the same specimen. For hospital-based laboratory surveillance, co-detection patterns provide information beyond single-pathogen positivity and add complexity to etiological attribution and laboratory interpretation. Accordingly, considering both single-pathogen temporal trends and multi-pathogen co-detection patterns may provide a more complete characterization of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity in the post-NPI period.4.3Pathogen-specific reshaping of detection patternsA central finding of this study is that pathogen detection patterns changed heterogeneously after the lifting of NPIs. Although many pathogen categories showed higher detection risks in the post-NPI period, the magnitude, timing, and stability of changes varied across pathogens. This pattern is consistent with reports of asynchronous respiratory virus resurgence and pathogen-specific recovery after relaxation of COVID-19-related restrictions (12, 14, 30). It supports the concept that the post-NPI period may represent pathogen-specific reshaping rather than a simple synchronized return to pre-pandemic seasonality. This distinction is important because aggregate respiratory pathogen positivity may obscure divergent trajectories among individual pathogens.Human rhinovirus showed the most statistically robust trend-related finding in our ITS analysis, with a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption and a positive post-NPI slope. This pattern is consistent with previous pediatric studies showing that rhinovirus activity was less suppressed by NPIs and could remain prominent or increase while several other respiratory viruses showed marked reductions or altered circulation (31–33). The positive association between school-term status and human rhinovirus positivity across age strata is also consistent with evidence that school sessions, holidays, and closures can influence respiratory infection activity in children (20, 34, 35). Thus, human rhinovirus may function as a sensitive indicator of renewed pediatric contact networks in the post-NPI period. Nevertheless, school-term status in this study was defined by calendar timing and should be interpreted as a population-level contextual indicator rather than a direct measure of individual school attendance, classroom exposure, or transmission pathway.Several pathogens, including human metapneumovirus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, and seasonal human coronaviruses, showed immediate level increases in the primary ITS model. Similar post-restriction shifts in human metapneumovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viruses have been reported after periods of reduced circulation or relaxation of COVID-19 restrictions (13, 36, 37). However, these signals in our study were attenuated after FDR correction, indicating lower statistical robustness under multiple-comparison control. These findings are still informative because they suggest transient post-NPI increases for several pathogens, while also showing that not all apparent rebounds were statistically stable after adjustment for multiple testing. For influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, the large period-comparison RR and wide confidence interval mainly reflected sparse detections during the NPI period, indicating a marked post-NPI increase with limited precision of the RR estimate.The RSV-focused supplementary analysis further highlights the translational relevance of age-specific surveillance, consistent with previous evidence that RSV contributes substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children and that RSV activity was altered during and after COVID-19-related restriction periods (2, 10–12). Although the primary age strata were designed to reflect childcare and schooling stages in China, reclassification into RSV prevention-relevant age windows showed that children younger than 2 years accounted for most RSV-positive records and had nearly twice the overall RSV detection risk observed in older children. The highest positivity was observed in the 6–<12-month and 12–<24-month groups, supporting the importance of infant- and toddler-focused RSV prevention and surveillance strategies. The stronger relative post-NPI increase among children aged ≥2 years also suggests broader age redistribution of RSV detection after the lifting of NPIs. Because this study was based on laboratory testing records, these findings should be interpreted as age-specific RSV detection patterns in a laboratory surveillance dataset and may inform future studies that link virological detection with hospitalization and severity outcomes.Human adenovirus showed a contrasting pattern, with both a lower post-NPI detection risk and a robust immediate level decrease in ITS analysis. This divergence from HRV further highlights the pathogen-specific nature of post-NPI changes. This pattern underscores the value of local pathogen-specific laboratory surveillance, because decreases in selected pathogens may be hidden when respiratory pathogen activity is assessed only through aggregate positivity. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionOver 5 years of continuous hospital-based laboratory surveillance, pediatric respiratory pathogen detection showed distinct overall and pathogen-specific patterns across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with higher overall positivity and co-detection rates in the post-NPI period. Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analyses further revealed different temporal trajectories, including an immediate decrease in HADV and a significant positive trend change in HRV with a positive post-NPI slope. Age-stratified analyses and assessments of meteorological and school-calendar factors further showed that associations between pathogen detection, age, and contextual factors were pathogen-specific; phase-interaction analyses additionally indicated that the associations of temperature with HPIV, school-term status with H3, and relative humidity with Ch differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Taken together, these findings support continued hospital-based multi-pathogen laboratory surveillance integrating pathogen-specific temporal trends, age stratification, co-detection patterns, and environmental and school-calendar context to facilitate dynamic identification of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity, prioritization of surveillance targets, and pediatric service preparedness.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionAcute respiratory infections remain a major cause of illness among children worldwide and are associated with substantial healthcare use, hospitalization, and public health burden (1). Among specific pediatric pathogens, respiratory syncytial virus, seasonal influenza virus, human metapneumovirus, and human parainfluenza virus contribute substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children (2–5). Laboratory-based surveillance in China has also shown that pediatric and community respiratory specimens can involve diverse viral and atypical pathogens rather than a single dominant target (6). These patterns vary by age, season, geography, and social contact structure, highlighting the importance of continuous laboratory-based surveillance for understanding temporal changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen activity.During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as mask wearing, school closures, reduced mobility, physical distancing, and enhanced hygiene measures, substantially altered community respiratory virus activity beyond SARS-CoV-2 (7). Observational and pediatric hospital-based studies in China showed broad impacts of NPIs on acute respiratory infections and common childhood respiratory viruses (8, 9). Respiratory syncytial virus-specific studies also reported altered epidemiological and clinical characteristics among hospitalized children during the pandemic period (10). These changes were not uniform across pathogens or regions, suggesting that pathogen biology, population susceptibility, testing behavior, and contact patterns may have interacted to shape observed laboratory detection trends.After the relaxation or lifting of COVID-19-related NPIs, many settings reported renewed activity of pediatric respiratory pathogens, but post-NPI changes have not consistently followed a single synchronized rebound pattern. Studies have described off-season or asynchronous resurgence of influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, and other common respiratory viruses after periods of reduced activity (11–13). Post-NPI resurgence or shifting epidemic features of Mycoplasma pneumoniae have also been reported in China and related pediatric studies (14, 15). The concept of immune debt has further been proposed to help explain heterogeneous pediatric respiratory infection activity after the pandemic (16). These observations suggest that the post-NPI period may be better understood as a phase of pathogen-specific reshaping of respiratory pathogen detection patterns rather than a simple return to pre-pandemic seasonality.In parallel with changes in population contact patterns, environmental and calendar-related factors may provide important context for respiratory pathogen activity. Temperature and meteorological conditions have been associated with viral seasonality and pathogen-specific acute respiratory infection patterns (17, 18). Air pollution has also been linked to respiratory infection susceptibility and pediatric respiratory health (19). School sessions have been associated with seasonal outbreaks of medically attended respiratory infections (20). Nevertheless, few studies have jointly evaluated meteorological conditions, air quality, and school-term status across multiple pediatric respiratory pathogen categories in the post-NPI period.Although evidence on post-NPI respiratory pathogen activity is increasing, the available literature remains constrained by several methodological limitations. Many studies have relied on short observation windows, selected-pathogen analyses, or simple before-and-after comparisons, which are insufficient to separate an abrupt post-policy level change from a sustained change in temporal slope. Continuous multi-year laboratory datasets that span both the NPI and post-NPI periods and simultaneously evaluate multiple pediatric respiratory pathogens remain scarce. Moreover, environmental conditions, air quality, and school-calendar context are rarely assessed within the same pathogen-specific analytical framework. These limitations restrict the ability of surveillance studies to determine whether post-NPI changes represent a uniform rebound or a more complex reshaping of pathogen-specific detection patterns.To address these gaps, we analyzed 20,250 pediatric throat-swab testing records collected over five consecutive years, from January 2021 to December 2025. We compared pathogen detection risks between the NPI and post-NPI periods, evaluated overall long-term and segmented temporal changes, applied pathogen-specific interrupted time-series models, and assessed associations of meteorological factors, air quality, and school-term status with pathogen-specific positivity, including potential variation in these associations across study periods. By integrating a large continuous laboratory dataset with time-series and contextual analyses, this study aimed to characterize pathogen-specific temporal patterns across the NPI and post-NPI periods and their relevance to hospital-based laboratory surveillance. 2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. papers.title_original: Ecological reshaping of pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles after COVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions were lifted: a 5-year interrupted time-series study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how the lifting of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) related to COVID-19 affected the ecological patterns of pediatric respiratory pathogens, particularly focusing on seasonal influenza viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This 5-year interrupted time-series study analyzed pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China, from 2018 to 2023. The study population included inpatients and neonates, with data stratified by age groups corresponding to infancy, early childhood, kindergarten age, and school age.
analysis.methods: Respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was conducted using a multiplex detection kit based on fluorescence PCR and capillary electrophoresis. The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories, and results were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals. Meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status were incorporated into multivariable logistic regression models.
analysis.main_results: Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis revealed heterogeneous patterns, with human adenovirus showing a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005) and human rhinovirus showing a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection before and after the lifting of NPIs, highlighting the complex interplay between public health measures and pathogen dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into how changes in public health policies can influence the detection rates of respiratory pathogens, which may inform future surveillance and intervention strategies for seasonal influenza viruses in pediatric populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design was limited to laboratory detection among tested inpatients and neonates, and it did not estimate community incidence or prevalence. The evidence is moderate due to the reliance on observational data and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This 5-year interrupted time-series study investigated the impact of lifting non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) related to COVID-19 on pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles, with a focus on seasonal influenza viruses. The study analyzed 13 respiratory pathogen categories using nucleic acid testing, multivariable logistic regression, and interrupted time-series models, incorporating meteorological factors and school-term status. Results showed heterogeneous patterns, with human adenovirus decreasing and human rhinovirus increasing in positivity after NPIs were lifted. Higher temperatures were linked to lower positivity of influenza A H1N1 (2009) and influenza B viruses, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. The authors interpreted these findings as reflecting distinct temporal patterns in pathogen detection, emphasizing the complex relationship between public health measures and viral dynamics. The study's significance lies in its potential to inform surveillance and intervention strategies for seasonal influenza in children. However, the evidence is moderate due to the study's focus on laboratory detection and the absence of community-level data.

news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-8-october-2026-week-41 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 40 of 2026 between 28 September and 4 October 2026. The main messages of this report are: influenza activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels COVID-19 activity increased and is circulating at low levels respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) activity remained low and is circulating at baseline levels Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents in the community was stable compared with the previous week. Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported for the first time this season. Data is for week 40 (up to 4 October 2026). Compared with the equivalent week last season (2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower in those aged 65 years and over, 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups, and 2 and 3-year-olds. Vaccine uptake is comparable for pregnant women. Some data relating to uptake in pharmacies was unavailable or incomplete at the time of reporting. Findings should be interpreted with caution, particularly in those aged 65 years or older, 6 months to under 65 years in risk groups and pregnant women, as results may be subject to change when additional data become available. COVID-19 activity increased across some indicators and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 40 2026 (week ending 4 October 2026) 10.2% of all people aged 75 years and over, and 4.1% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system, had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity remained low and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis remained low and below seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 4 October 2026, there were a total of 1,638 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 40, increasing from 1,328 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings increased in week 40, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 9.1% up to Sunday 4 October 2026 compared with 7.9% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 13.1% up to Sunday 4 October 2026. This has increased compared to 10.4% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity increased in week 40, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.5% up to Sunday 4 October 2026. This is compared with 5.0% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased in week 40, with a rolling 7 day positivity rate of 5.8% up to Sunday 4 October 2026. Influenza B positivity increased in the same week, with a rolling 7 day positivity rate of 0.4% up to Sunday 4 October 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 18 and 24 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 28.1% up to Sunday 4 October 2026. This has increased from 24.4% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.5%. This has decreased slightly from 1.6% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Due to an ongoing data quality issue resulting in more tests than usual being removed, historical positivity for influenza may be slightly lower in reports published from week 25 2026 onwards. Historical estimates will be updated once the affected data has been rectified. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 40, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.5% up to Sunday 4 October 2026, compared with 0.4% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 3.5% up to Sunday 4 October 2026 in week 40. This has increased from 2.4% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 40, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 40, 2,765 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 156 positive samples for influenza: 88 influenza A (not subtyped), 40 influenza A (H3N2), 18 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 12 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased slightly to 5.6% in week 40 compared with 5.3% in the previous week. In week 40, 3,396 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 258 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity increased slightly to 7.6% compared with 6.8% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 10.6%. RSV positivity increased to 0.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 4.4%. Adenovirus positivity decreased to 0.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 4.4%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity decreased to 0.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 0.5%. Parainfluenza positivity increased slightly to 2.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.7%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 17.3%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 34.4%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 31 August 2026 and 13 September 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell and egg based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses show that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 40 2026 (week ending 4 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 92 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 44 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 41 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 7 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has not yet confirmed the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in any influenza A/B positive sample, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years of age by genome sequencing. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared to reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been no detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility or resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Please note that reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 114 new ARI incidents reported in week 40 in England. These included: 99 incidents from care homes, of which 21 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 12 were due to influenza A, 5 were due to other pathogens and 1 was due to multiple pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 60 incidents 6 incidents from hospitals, of which 4 were due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza A. No pathogen was reported in 1 incident 1 incident from educational settings for which no tests were available 8 incidents from other settings, of which 4 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 1 was due to influenza A and 1 was due to multiple pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 2 incidents Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 04 October 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable. ED attendance for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) were stable and below seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls continued to increase in line with seasonally expected baselines. Increases in calls and online assessments for acute respiratory infection stabilised in children aged up to 14 years during the past week, but continued to increase in older age groups over 15 years. GP in-hours consultation rates for upper respiratory tract infections increased, most notably in adults aged over 45 years but broadly in line with seasonal expectations. There were further increases in COVID-19-like consultation rates. Influenza-like illness consultation rates increased and were above levels expected for the time of year with increases noted in adults, particularly those aged 15 to 44 years. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for ‘acute respiratory infections’ and ‘difficulty breathing or wheeze or asthma’ increased in line with seasonally expected baselines. Both of these indicators were stable or decreased in the under 15 years age groups but increased in the over 15 years age groups. Daily influenza-like illness contacts stabilised nationally. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance increased to 5.6 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 40 compared with 4.0 per 100,000 in the previous week. This rate is in the baseline activity level (Figure 20). By age group, the highest rates were seen in those aged between 15 and 44 years (7.2 per 100,000), and those aged between 1 and 4 years (5.3 per 100,000). The lower respiratory tract infections ( LRTI ) consultation rate increased to 79.5 per 100,000 in week 40 compared with 70.3 per 100,000 in the previous week. Further details are available in the weekly RSC communicable and respiratory disease report for England . MEM thresholds are based on data from the 2018 to 2019 season to the 2025 to 2026 season. Note the 2019 to 2020, 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022 seasons have been removed. From week 40 2025, the RCGP sentinel swabbing scheme testing capability has been expanded to the UKHSA Bristol laboratory in addition to the UKHSA Colindale laboratory. Samples sent to Colindale are tested for influenza A and B, RSV…

analysis.location_and_population: The report is focused on England, with data on influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and COVID-19 activity across various populations, including those aged 75 years and over, individuals with weakened immune systems, and specific age groups such as 65 years and over, 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups, and 2 and 3-year-olds.
analysis.event: The report indicates that influenza activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 8 October 2026 (week 41) outlines the status of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and COVID-19 in England. Influenza activity increased, with emergency department (ED) attendances for influenza-like-illness (ILI) above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents in the community remained stable compared to the previous week. Vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported, with lower rates observed in certain age groups and risk groups. The report highlights that findings should be interpreted with caution, especially for those aged 65 years or older, individuals in clinical risk groups, and pregnant women. Data on RSV activity remained low, and ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis were below expected levels. The report also notes that some data on pharmacy uptake was incomplete, and the methods used for defining activity levels, such as MEM and MSD, may be subject to future revisions. The surveillance data is based on information up to week 40 of 2026, which ended on 4 October 2026.

Health Assembly Executive Board Member States Portal Home/ Publications/ Overview/ Global Respiratory Virus Activity: Weekly Update N° 598 Global Respiratory Virus Activity: Weekly Update N° 598 Week 39, ending 27 September 2026 7 October 2026 | Emergency situation update Download (5.8 MB) Overview In week 39 2026, globally, influenza positivity was below 10% and SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low. Influenza positivity was below 10% in the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas and at 10% in the tropical areas. Influenza positivity was below 10% in the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas with a decrease in the reported specimens tested in the most recent week. RSV positivity also remained low globally. Influenza Globally, influenza detections remained low in week 39 with influenza A virus detections predominant. An increase in the proportion of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 detections has been observed over recent weeks. In the southern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in single countries in Tropical and Temperate South America and Eastern Africa. Percent positivity was over 30% in single countries in South-East Asia and Oceania. Increases in activity were reported in single countries in Temperate South America and South-East Asia. In the northern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in some countries in Western Africa, Southern, South-East and Eastern Asia and in a single country in Central America and the Caribbean and Western Asia. Percent positivity was over 30% in some countries in Western, Southern and South-East Asia and in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Western Africa. Increases in activity were observed in some countries in Western and South-East Asia and in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Western Africa and Southern Asia. In the zones with elevated positivity, influenza A(H3N2) was predominant in Eastern Asia; influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 was predominant in Western, Southern and South-East Asia and influenza B was predominant in Tropical and Temperate South America. Influenza A and B were codominant in Central America and the Caribbean and Western Africa and influenza A(H3N2) and influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 were codominant in Oceania. SARS-CoV-2 Globally, SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low across most reporting countries, with elevated positivity (>10%) reported in some countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Eastern Asia, and in single countries in South West and Northern Europe and South-East Asia. A medium increase in activity was observed in a single country in Central America and the Caribbean, and small increases in activity were observed in single countries in South West and Eastern Europe. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) RSV positivity was elevated (>10%) in a few countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Temperate South America and in a single country in Tropical South America. Percent positivity was over 30% in a single country in Southern Asia. A small increase in activity was observed in a single country in Central America and the Caribbean. RSV and influenza activity were both elevated in countries in Temperate South America and Southern Asia. Severity assessment The severity assessments here are reported from countries, areas and territories. Assessments for transmissibility can be reported based on syndromic parameters and/or influenza-specific parameters. In the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country and low in a single country; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country. In the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in 13 countries, low in a single country and moderate in a single country; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in eight countries and low in a single country. Influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country in the tropical areas. WHO encourages countries, especially those that have received the multiplex influenza and SARS-CoV-2 reagent kits from GISRS, to conduct integrated surveillance of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 and report epidemiological and laboratory information in a timely manner to established regional and global platforms. The guidance can be found here. Starting with report #501, the Global Respiratory Virus Activity Weekly Update included data from sentinel surveillance and other types of systematically conducted virologic surveillance. Countries, areas, and territories use a variety of approaches to monitor respiratory virus activity and data in this report may vary from surveillance reports posted elsewhere. Analyses stratified by source of surveillance is available through Respimart. supplementary_news.content: https://ukhsa.blog.gov.uk/2026/10/08/are-we-seeing-an-early-flu-season-what-we-know-so-far-about-this-years-strains/ Early signs suggest that flu season may be starting earlier this year. According to our winter virus surveillance data , flu activity throughout September has been higher than in the same period over the past 4 winters. While levels remain at baseline, meaning still relatively low overall, the upward trend - if it continues in the coming weeks - suggests an early flu season. The rise so far has been driven largely by cases in the 18- to 24-year-old age group. What strains are circulating this year? So far this season, there's a mix of 2 flu A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2, circulating in England. The flu vaccine is designed to protect against all 3 main types of flu: influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and influenza B. Whichever ends up dominating this winter - or if they all circulate at similar levels throughout - the vaccine should offer broad protection. It might help to think of the flu vaccine like packing for a winter trip: you bring layers for rain, snow and wind because you don't know exactly what the weather will throw at you. The vaccine works the same way, offering layered protection against all 3 flu types so you're prepared, whatever ends up circulating. What is a 'drifted' strain? Flu viruses are constantly changing through a natural process called antigenic drift. Each year, the World Health Organization monitors circulating strains globally and selects which ones should be targeted by that season's vaccine, but this decision has to be made months in advance, to give manufacturers time to produce enough doses. Sometimes the virus continues to change after that point, resulting in it no longer matching the vaccine strain as closely as originally predicted. This year, it's the A(H1N1) subtype that has drifted from the strain used in the vaccine . It's still too early in the season to know for certain whether this drifted H1N1 will circulate widely in the UK, or how it will affect vaccine effectiveness. How does this compare to last winter? Last winter, a drifted strain of H3N2, known as subclade K, emerged after the vaccine composition for the Northern Hemisphere had already been finalised. Despite this, the vaccine was effective and even with an earlier start to the flu season, overall levels of activity and mortality were lower than the previous year. Modelling suggests the vaccination programme in England prevented around 100,000 hospital admissions and 7,000 deaths that winter. Does the vaccine still work against drifted strains? Drift is a normal and expected part of how flu viruses behave, and experience shows that vaccines typically remain effective at preventing severe illness even when the circulating strain doesn't perfectly match the one used to make the vaccine. Our analysis from last season found vaccinated children were around 65 to 70% less likely to attend or be admitted to hospital with flu, while vaccinated adults were around 20 to 30% less likely. Does this affect when I should get vaccinated? Because flu activity is already trending higher than usual for this point in the year, and because it takes a couple of weeks for the vaccine to provide full protection, getting vaccinated sooner rather than later gives you the best chance of being protected before flu takes hold more widely. If this does turn into an early season, waiting could mean you're exposed during the period before your immunity has had time to build. What's UKHSA doing to keep track of this? UKHSA is continuing to monitor the drifted H1N1 strain through laboratory analysis, routine surveillance of flu's impact on health, and ongoing studies into how well the vaccine is working in practice. This monitoring will continue throughout winter, including watching for any other strains that start to become more prominent. What should I do now? If you're eligible for a free flu vaccine , the advice is simple: don't wait. You can check your eligibility and book an appointment through the NHS App, online, or by contacting your GP practice or a local pharmacy. For school-aged children, most vaccines are delivered in schools by local immunisation teams. Look out for consent forms and return them. Community clinics are available for children who miss school sessions. From 1 December 2026, school-aged children from Reception to Year 11 who did not get vaccinated in school can also get vaccinated at a pharmacy . Given the early signs this season, getting protected now, rather than later, is the best way to guard against serious illness this winter. Tags: flu , H1N1 , H3N2 , influenza , vaccination

supplementary_news.content: Search | RU | EN | KG | Home News Local newsEconomyIncidentsExclusiveHealthSportsEcology About Kyrgyzstan Weather Advertising on the Website Weather Home News Local newsEconomyIncidentsExclusiveHealthSportsEcology About Kyrgyzstan For Tourists Home » News » In the world » Five cases of seasonal flu registered in Kazakhstan, - Ministry of Health Five cases of seasonal flu registered in Kazakhstan, - Ministry of Health Евгения Комарова • 09.10.2026, 17:03 • In the world Discover more health Health Get Health Tips Read on Telegram Read on Facebook Five cases of seasonal influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 have been confirmed in Kazakhstan, according to information from the Ministry of Health. Over the past week, the incidence of ARVI has decreased by 10.2%. According to epidemiological monitoring data, three cases of influenza were registered in the capital, Astana, and two in the Mangistau region. A total of 834 samples were analyzed as part of the study, of which five tested positive. In the past week, the country recorded 127,266 cases of ARVI, which is 13,007 fewer compared to the previous week when 140,273 cases were registered. Since the beginning of September, the total number of cases has reached 760,182. Additionally, 68 cases of rhinovirus infection, 47 cases of coronavirus infections, 50 cases of bocavirus infection, 32 cases of parainfluenza, 27 cases of adenovirus infection, two cases of respiratory syncytial infection, and one case of metapneumovirus infection have been identified in Kazakhstan. The Ministry of Health also emphasized that 2.1 million doses of the "Grippol Plus" vaccine have been purchased for free vaccination of the population against influenza. The vaccine is available in all regions of the country, and as of October 7, 240,375 people have been vaccinated.
